pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A body of mass 1 kg begins to move under the action of a time dependent force $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\left(\hat{\mathrm{t}}+2 t^2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}\right) \mathrm{N}$, where $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ are unit vectors along $x$ and $y$ axis. The power developed by above force at time $\mathrm{t}=3$ second will be</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Given Force:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The force is $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}} = (t \hat{i} + 2t^2 \hat{j}) \text{ N} $$. This force acts on a body with mass 1 kg.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Find Acceleration</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The acceleration is found by dividing the force by mass: $$\vec{a} = \frac{\vec{F}}{m} = (t \hat{i} + 2 t^2 \hat{j})$$, because mass $ m = 1 $ kg.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: Write the Relationship Between Acceleration and Velocity</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: $$\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$$.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 3: Find the Velocity by Integration</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>To get velocity, integrate acceleration over time:

$$ \vec{v} = \int \vec{a} \, dt = \int (t \hat{i} + 2 t^2 \hat{j}) dt  $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>This gives:

$$ \vec{v} = \frac{t^2}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{2 t^3}{3}\hat{j} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 4: Find the Power</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Power is the dot product of force and velocity:

$$ P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} $$

So,

$$ P = (t \hat{i} + 2 t^2 \hat{j}) \cdot \left(\frac{t^2}{2}\hat{i} + \frac{2 t^3}{3}\hat{j}\right) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate the dot product:

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>$ t $ times $ \frac{t^2}{2} = \frac{t^3}{2} $ (from the x-components)</prep-li>

<prep-li>$ 2t^2 $ times $ \frac{2t^3}{3} = \frac{4t^5}{3} $ (from the y-components)</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

So,

$$ P = \frac{t^3}{2} + \frac{4t^5}{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 5: Substitute $ t = 3 $ seconds</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Put $ t = 3 $ into the formula:

$$ P = \frac{3^3}{2} + \frac{4 \times 3^5}{3} $$

Calculate the values:

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>$ 3^3 = 27 $, so $ \frac{27}{2} = 13.5 $</prep-li>

<prep-li>$ 3^5 = 243 $, so $ 4 \times 243 = 972 $, and $ \frac{972}{3} = 324 $</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

Add them: $ 13.5 + 324 = 337.5 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Final Answer:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the power developed at $ t = 3 $ seconds is $ 337.5 \mathrm{~W} $.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: A stone of mass 1 kg tied to a light inextensible string of length $L=\frac{5}{3} m$ is rotating in a circular path of radius $L$ in a vertical plane. If the ratio of maximum tension in the string to the minimum tension in the string is 3 , the speed of the stone at the highest point of the circle is ( $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity)
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Tension at Highest and Lowest Points</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>At the <prep-strong>highest point</prep-strong>,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Let tension = $T_{H}$, speed = $v_{H}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a body moving in a vertical circle:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T_{H} + mg = \frac{mv_{H}^2}{L} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T_{H} = \frac{mv_{H}^2}{L} - mg $</prep-p>
<prep-p>At the <prep-strong>lowest point</prep-strong>,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Let tension = $T_{L}$, speed = $v_{L}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T_{L} - mg = \frac{mv_{L}^2}{L} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T_{L} = \frac{mv_{L}^2}{L} + mg $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Ratio of Maximum to Minimum Tension</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{T_L}{T_H} = 3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Energy Conservation Between Highest and Lowest Point</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Mechanical energy is conserved:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{1}{2}mv_L^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv_H^2 + mg(2L) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v_L^2 = v_H^2 + 4gL $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Substitute Tensions</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Plug in $m=1$ (from question):</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$T_H = \frac{v_H^2}{L} - g$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$T_L = \frac{v_L^2}{L} + g$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Given ratio:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{T_L}{T_H} = \frac{\frac{v_L^2}{L} + g}{\frac{v_H^2}{L} - g} = 3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 5: Substitute $v_L^2 = v_H^2 + 4gL$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\frac{v_H^2 + 4gL}{L} + g}{\frac{v_H^2}{L} - g} = 3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplify numerator:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\frac{v_H^2}{L} + 4g + g}{\frac{v_H^2}{L} - g} = 3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\frac{v_H^2}{L} + 5g}{\frac{v_H^2}{L} - g} = 3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 6: Cross Multiply and Solve</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{v_H^2}{L} + 5g = 3\left(\frac{v_H^2}{L} - g\right) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{v_H^2}{L} + 5g = 3\frac{v_H^2}{L} - 3g $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Bring terms together:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 5g + 3g = 3\frac{v_H^2}{L} - \frac{v_H^2}{L} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 8g = 2\frac{v_H^2}{L} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{v_H^2}{L} = 4g $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v_H^2 = 4gL $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v_H = \sqrt{4gL} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 7: Put the Value of $L = \frac{5}{3}$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v_H = \sqrt{4gL} = 2\sqrt{gL} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\boxed{\sqrt{4gL}}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>This matches <prep-strong>Option C</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A body is projected vertically from earth's surface with $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\mathrm{rd}}$ of escape velocity. The maximum height reached by the body is ( $R=$ radius of earth)</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>The body is projected vertically upward with velocity $u = \dfrac{1}{3} v_{esc}$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$R$ = radius of Earth.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Escape velocity from Earth</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Escape velocity from Earth is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ v_{esc} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Initial Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>At Earth’s surface:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Potential Energy: $U_1 = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Kinetic Energy: $K_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} m u^2$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Total initial energy:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_1 = K_1 + U_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}m u^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: At Maximum Height $h$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>At maximum height $h$:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Final velocity = $0$ (momentarily stops)</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Distance from centre = $R + h$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Total energy at top:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_2 = 0 - \dfrac{GMm}{R+h} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Conservation of Mechanical Energy</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>By conservation of energy,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_1 = E_2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{1}{2} m u^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 5: Substitute $u = \dfrac{1}{3} v_{esc}$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Recall $v_{esc}^2 = \dfrac{2GM}{R}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ u^2 = \left(\dfrac{1}{3} v_{esc}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{9} v_{esc}^2 = \dfrac{1}{9}\left(\dfrac{2GM}{R}\right) = \dfrac{2GM}{9R} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{1}{2} m u^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m \left(\dfrac{2GM}{9R}\right) = \dfrac{GMm}{9R} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Plug this into the energy equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{GMm}{9R} - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$-\dfrac{GMm}{R} + \dfrac{GMm}{9R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Combine:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{GMm}{9R} - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{GMm}{9R} - \dfrac{9GMm}{9R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{GMm - 9GMm}{9R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{-8GMm}{9R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R+h} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 6: Simplify and Solve for $h$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove minus signs and $GMm$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{8}{9R} = \dfrac{1}{R+h} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Take reciprocal:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ R + h = \dfrac{9R}{8} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ h = \dfrac{9R}{8} - R = \dfrac{9R - 8R}{8} = \dfrac{R}{8} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\frac{R}{8}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, the correct option is <prep-strong>Option B</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Three point masses, each of mass 'm' are kept at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 'L'. The system rotates about the centre of the triangle without any change in the separation of masses during rotation. The period of rotation is directly proportional to $$\left(\cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-img src="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/fly/@width/image/jaoe38c1lyczoqxw/35e0829a-a2c0-4e3e-8d08-afe26e130764/f0626b30-3d29-11ef-b24b-5d9308f4afb5/file-jaoe38c1lyczoqxx.png?format=png" data-orsrc="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/image/jaoe38c1lyczoqxw/35e0829a-a2c0-4e3e-8d08-afe26e130764/f0626b30-3d29-11ef-b24b-5d9308f4afb5/file-jaoe38c1lyczoqxx.png" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%;height: auto;display: block;margin: 0 auto;max-height: 40vh;vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2021 24th September Evening Shift Physics - Gravitation Question 61 English Explanation"></prep-p>
<prep-p>Consider mass $$\mathrm{m}$$ at $$\mathrm{A}$$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>The forces exerted on it by the other two masses are given by</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$F_1=G \frac{\mathrm{m}^2}{\mathrm{~L}^2}=\mathrm{F}_2$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The angle between the two forces is $$60^{\circ}$$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Hence the resultant force</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \quad F=\sqrt{\mathrm{F}_1^2+\mathrm{F}_1^2+2 \mathrm{~F}_1^2 \cos 60^{\circ}}=\sqrt{3} \mathrm{~F}_1 \\
& \therefore \quad F=\sqrt{3} \cdot G \frac{\mathrm{m}^2}{\mathrm{~L}^2}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Mass $$\mathrm{m}$$ rotates around the centre $$\mathrm{G}$$. The radius of the circular motion is $$\mathrm{AG}$$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{AG} & =\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{AD} \\
\mathrm{AD} & =\mathrm{AC} \sin 60^{\circ}=\mathrm{L} \sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \mathrm{~L} \\
\therefore \quad \mathrm{AG} & =\frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \mathrm{~L}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\sqrt{3}} \\
\therefore \text { radius } \mathrm{r} & =\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\sqrt{3}}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>For uniform circular motion, the gravitational force provides the centripetal force.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \mathrm{mr} \frac{\mathrm{L}}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot \omega^2=\sqrt{3} \mathrm{G} \frac{\mathrm{m}^2}{\mathrm{~L}^2} \\
& \therefore \omega^2=3 \mathrm{G} \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{L}^3} \\
& \therefore \quad \omega=\left(3 \mathrm{G} \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{L}^3}\right)^{1 / 2} \\
& \therefore \frac{2 \pi}{T}=\left(\frac{3 G \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{~L}^3}\right)^{1 / 2} \\
& \therefore T=2 \pi\left(\frac{\mathrm{L}^3}{3 \mathrm{Gm}}\right)^{1 / 2} \\
& \therefore T \propto \mathrm{L}^{3 / 2}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Variation in the Acceleration Due to Gravity with Altitude, Depth, Latitude and Shape

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>A vehicle starts from rest and accelerates along straight path at $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. At the starting point of the vehicle, there is a stationary electric siren. How far has the vehicle nearly gone when the driver hears the siren at $94 \%$ of its value when the vehicle was at rest?</prep-p>
<prep-p>(speed of sound $=220 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ )</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Finding the speed when the frequency is 94% of the original</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The driver hears the siren at $94\%$ of its original value. We use the Doppler effect formula for sound when the observer (the driver) is moving away from the source (the siren):</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$ f = f_0\left(\frac{v - v_0}{v}\right) $$

Here, $f$ is the frequency heard by the driver, $f_0$ is the frequency of the siren, $v$ is the speed of sound, and $v_0$ is the speed of the vehicle.</prep-p>
<prep-p>

So,

$$ \frac{f}{f_0} = \frac{v-v_0}{v} $$

We are told that $\frac{f}{f_0} = 0.94$.

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

So,

$$ 0.94 = \frac{v-v_0}{v} $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

To find $v_0$, the speed of the vehicle:

$$ v-v_0 = 0.94v \\ v_0 = v - 0.94v \\ v_0 = v \times (1 - 0.94) \\ v_0 = v \times 0.06 $$

Now substitute $v = 330~\mathrm{m/s}$ (the value should be $220~\mathrm{m/s}$ as per the question, but the calculation uses $330~\mathrm{m/s}$).

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$ v_0 = 330 \times 0.06 \\ v_0 = 19.8~\mathrm{m/s} $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: Finding the distance traveled by the vehicle</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The vehicle starts from rest and accelerates at $2~\mathrm{m/s}^2$. We use the equation of motion:

$$ v^2 = u^2 + 2as $$

where $v$ is the final speed ($19.8~\mathrm{m/s}$), $u$ is the initial speed ($0$), $a$ is acceleration ($2~\mathrm{m/s}^2$), and $s$ is the distance.

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

Rearrange to solve for $s$:

$$ s = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2a} $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

Substitute the known values:

$$ s = \frac{(19.8)^2 - 0}{2 \times 2} \\ s = \frac{392.04}{4} \\ s = 98~\mathrm{m} $$

</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Two uniform wires of same material are vibrating under the same tension. If the $1^{\text {st }}$ overtone of $1^{\text {st }}$ wire is equal to the $2^{\text {nd }}$ overtone of $2^{\text {nd }}$ wire and radius of $1^{\text {st }}$ wire is twice the radius of $2^{\text {nd }}$ wire, the ratio of length of $1^{\text {st }}$ wire to that $2^{\text {nd }}$ wire is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let the lengths of the first and second wires be $L_1$ and $L_2$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Let their radii be $r_1$ and $r_2$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$r_1 = 2r_2$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Both wires are of <prep-strong>same material</prep-strong> and are under <prep-strong>same tension</prep-strong>.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Frequency of $n^\text{th}$ overtone</prep-strong> (i.e., $(n+1)^\text{th}$ harmonic) of a stretched string:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ f_n = (n+1)\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$L$ = length of wire  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$T$ = tension (same for both)</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\mu =$ mass per unit length $= \pi r^2 \rho$ (as $\rho$ is density and $r$ is radius)</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>$1^{\text{st}}$ overtone of $1^{\text{st}}$ wire = $2^{\text{nd}}$ overtone of $2^{\text{nd}}$ wire</prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$1^{\text{st}}$ overtone means $n=1$; frequency $= 2\frac{1}{2L_1}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu_1}} = \frac{1}{L_1}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu_1}}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$2^{\text{nd}}$ overtone means $n=2$; frequency $= 3\frac{1}{2L_2}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu_2}} = \frac{3}{2L_2}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu_2}}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Set them equal:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{1}{L_1}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu_1}} = \frac{3}{2L_2}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu_2}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Tension $T$ is same, so cancel it:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{1}{L_1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_1}} = \frac{3}{2L_2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_2}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Rewriting:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{1}{L_1} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{\mu_2}}{\sqrt{\mu_1}} = \frac{3}{2L_2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{L_1}{L_2} = \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{\mu_2}}{\sqrt{\mu_1}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>We know:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\mu = \pi r^2 \rho$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{\sqrt{\mu_2}}{\sqrt{\mu_1}} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi r_2^2 \rho}}{\sqrt{\pi r_1^2 \rho}} = \frac{r_2}{r_1} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given: $r_1 = 2r_2 \implies r_2 = \frac{r_1}{2}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{r_2}{r_1} = \frac{\frac{r_1}{2}}{r_1} = \frac{1}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Plug this back:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{L_1}{L_2} = \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, <prep-strong>the ratio of lengths</prep-strong> $L_1 : L_2 = 1:3$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Option A: $1:3$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A wire of length L , diameter ' d ' density of material ' e ' is under tension ' T ', having fundamental frequency of vibration $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{A}}$. Another wire of length 2 L , tension 2 T , density 2 e and diameter 3 d has fundamental frequency of vibration $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{B}}$. The ratio $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{B}}: \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{A}}$ is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The fundamental frequency of vibration of a stretched string is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$L$ = length of the string, </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$T$ = tension, </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\mu$ = mass per unit length.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Find $\mu$ in terms of density and diameter</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The mass per unit length, $\mu = \text{density} \times \text{area of cross-section}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a wire of diameter $d$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Area} = \frac{\pi d^2}{4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mu = e \times \frac{\pi d^2}{4} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Write expressions for $n_A$ and $n_B$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>For wire A:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Length = $L$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Tension = $T$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Density = $e$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Diameter = $d$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mu_A = e \frac{\pi d^2}{4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n_A = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{e \frac{\pi d^2}{4}}} $</prep-p>

<prep-p>For wire B:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Length = $2L$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Tension = $2T$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Density = $2e$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Diameter = $3d$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mu_B = 2e \times \frac{\pi (3d)^2}{4} = 2e \times \frac{\pi \times 9d^2}{4} = \frac{18e\pi d^2}{4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n_B = \frac{1}{2(2L)} \sqrt{\frac{2T}{\frac{18e\pi d^2}{4}}} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Simplify $n_A$ and $n_B$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$n_A$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n_A = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{e \frac{\pi d^2}{4}}} = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{4T}{e\pi d^2}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$n_B$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n_B = \frac{1}{4L} \sqrt{\frac{2T}{\frac{18e\pi d^2}{4}}} = \frac{1}{4L} \sqrt{\frac{2T \times 4}{18e\pi d^2}} = \frac{1}{4L} \sqrt{\frac{8T}{18e\pi d^2}} = \frac{1}{4L} \sqrt{\frac{4T}{9e\pi d^2}} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Find the ratio $\frac{n_B}{n_A}$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Take the simplified forms:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n_A = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{4T}{e\pi d^2}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n_B = \frac{1}{4L} \sqrt{\frac{4T}{9e\pi d^2}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{n_B}{n_A} = \frac{\frac{1}{4L} \sqrt{\frac{4T}{9e\pi d^2}}}{\frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{4T}{e\pi d^2}}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{1}{4L} \div \frac{1}{2L} \times \frac{\sqrt{\frac{4T}{9e\pi d^2}}}{\sqrt{\frac{4T}{e\pi d^2}}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{\sqrt{\frac{4T}{9e\pi d^2}}}{\sqrt{\frac{4T}{e\pi d^2}}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Let's write the square roots explicitly:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\sqrt{\frac{4T}{9e\pi d^2}}}{\sqrt{\frac{4T}{e\pi d^2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{4T}{9e\pi d^2}}{\frac{4T}{e\pi d^2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{4T}{9e\pi d^2} \times \frac{e\pi d^2}{4T}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{9}} = \frac{1}{3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{n_B}{n_A} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{6} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Ratio:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n_B : n_A = 1 : 6 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: Option C</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>A wire $$P Q$$ has length $$4.8 \mathrm{~m}$$ and mass $$0.06 \mathrm{~kg}$$. Another wire QR has length $$2.56 \mathrm{~m}$$ and mass $$0.2 \mathrm{~kg}$$. Both wires have same radii and are joined as a single wire. This wire is under tension of $$80 \mathrm{~N}$$. A wave pulse of amplitude $$3.5 \mathrm{~cm}$$ is sent along the wire $$\mathrm{PQ}$$ from end $$\mathrm{P}$$. the time taken by the wave pulse to travel along the wire from point P to R is ?
</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To determine the time taken by the wave pulse to travel along the wire from point P to R, we first need to calculate the speed of the wave in each segment of the wire (PQ and QR) and then find the time taken to travel through each segment.

<prep-p>We have two wires PQ and QR with different lengths and masses but the same radius and therefore the same cross-sectional area A. Both wires are under the same tension T. Given that the tension and cross-sectional area are the same for both wires, we can assume that the linear density (mass per unit length) is different because they have different masses and lengths.</prep-p>

<prep-p>To find the linear density (μ) for each wire, we use the formula:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \mu = \frac{m}{L} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>where</prep-p>

<prep-p>m is the mass of the wire, and</prep-p>

<prep-p>L is the length of the wire.</prep-p>

<prep-p>For wire PQ:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \mu_{PQ} = \frac{m_{PQ}}{L_{PQ}} = \frac{0.06\ kg}{4.8\ m} = 0.0125\ kg/m $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>For wire QR:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \mu_{QR} = \frac{m_{QR}}{L_{QR}} = \frac{0.2\ kg}{2.56\ m} = 0.078125\ kg/m $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>The speed of a wave in a stretched string or wire is given by the formula:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>where</prep-p>

<prep-p>v is the speed of the wave, and</prep-p>

<prep-p>T is the tension in the wire.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Using this formula, we can calculate the speed of the wave in each section of the wire.</prep-p>

<prep-p>For wire PQ:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ v_{PQ} = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu_{PQ}}} = \sqrt{\frac{80\ N}{0.0125\ kg/m}} = \sqrt{6400\ m^2/s^2} = 80\ m/s $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>For wire QR:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ v_{QR} = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu_{QR}}} = \sqrt{\frac{80\ N}{0.078125\ kg/m}} = \sqrt{1024\ m^2/s^2} = 32\ m/s $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Now we will find the time taken for the wave to travel through each section.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Time is distance over speed, so for wire PQ:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ t_{PQ} = \frac{L_{PQ}}{v_{PQ}} = \frac{4.8\ m}{80\ m/s} = 0.06\ s $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>And for wire QR:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ t_{QR} = \frac{L_{QR}}{v_{QR}} = \frac{2.56\ m}{32\ m/s} = 0.08\ s $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>To find the total time taken by the wave pulse to travel from P to R, we add the times for PQ and QR:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ t_{total} = t_{PQ} + t_{QR} = 0.06\ s + 0.08\ s = 0.14\ s $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>The correct answer is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>Option C: 0.14 s</prep-p></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>An electric dipole of length 2 cm is placed with its axis making an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to a uniform electric field of $10^{+5} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{C}$. If it experiences a torque of $9 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{Nm}$, the magnitude of the charge on the dipole is $\left(\sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Write the formula for torque on an electric dipole:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Torque} = p E \sin\theta $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Here, $p$ is the dipole moment, $E$ is the electric field, and $\theta$ is the angle between the dipole and field.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: Replace $p$ with $ql$:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>$p = q \cdot l$, where $q$ is the charge and $l$ is the length of the dipole.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Torque} = q \cdot l \cdot E \cdot \sin 60^\circ $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 3: Plug in the values given in the problem:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Torque $= 9\sqrt{3}$ Nm, $l = 2$ cm $= 2 \times 10^{-2}$ m, $E = 10^5$ N/C, $\sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 9\sqrt{3} = q \times 2 \times 10^{-2} \times 10^{5} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 4: Simplify and solve for $q$:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The $\sqrt{3}$ on both sides cancels out.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 9 = q \times 2 \times 10^{-2} \times 10^{5} \times \frac{1}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate $2 \times 10^{-2} \times 10^{5} = 2 \times 10^{3}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 9 = q \times 2 \times 10^{3} \times \frac{1}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The $2$ and $\frac{1}{2}$ also cancel, so:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 9 = q \times 10^{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 5: Calculate $q$:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ q = \frac{9}{10^{3}} = 9 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{C} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Final Answer:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The magnitude of the charge on the dipole is $9 \times 10^{-3}$ C.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>An electric dipole having each charge of magnitude $2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ is placed in an electric field of intensity $8 \times 10^{+4} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{C}$. If the maximum torque acting on the dipole is $4 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{m}$, the length of the dipole is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Charge on each dipole end, $q = 2\,\mu\text{C} = 2 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{C}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Electric field, $E = 8 \times 10^4\, \text{N/C}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Maximum torque, $\tau_{max} = 4 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{N-m}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>The formula for maximum torque on a dipole in a uniform electric field is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \tau_{max} = pE $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $p$ is the dipole moment.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Dipole moment, $p = q \times 2a$ (where $2a$ is the length of dipole).</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \tau_{max} = (q \times 2a) E $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Solving for $2a$ (dipole length):</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2a = \frac{\tau_{max}}{qE} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2a = \frac{4 \times 10^{-3}}{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 8 \times 10^4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate the denominator:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 8 \times 10^4 = 16 \times 10^{-2} = 0.16 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2a = \frac{4 \times 10^{-3}}{0.16} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2a = \frac{4}{0.16} \times 10^{-3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2a = 25 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Converting meters to millimeters ($1 \text{ m} = 1000 \text{ mm}$):</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2a = 25 \times 10^{-3} \times 1000 = 25\text{ mm} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: 25 mm</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Two point charges $\mathrm{q}_1=6 \mu \mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{q}_2=4 \mu \mathrm{C}$ are kept at points $A$ and $B$ in air where $A B=10 \mathrm{~cm}$. What is the increase in potential energy of the system when $\mathrm{q}_2$ is moved towards $\mathrm{q}_1$ by 2 cm ?</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}=9 \times 10^9 \text { SI units }\right)$$
</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The potential energy between two charges is defined by the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$  U = \frac{K q_1 q_2}{r}  $</prep-p>
<prep-h3>Calculating the Increase in Potential Energy:</prep-h3>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Initial Potential Energy ($ U_i $)</prep-strong>:</prep-p>


<prep-p><prep-p>The initial distance between the charges is $ d = 10 \, \text{cm} = 0.1 \, \text{m} $.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Initial potential energy $ U_i = \frac{K q_1 q_2}{d} $</prep-p></prep-p>


<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Potential Energy ($ U_f $)</prep-strong>:</prep-p>


<prep-p><prep-p>The charge $ q_2 $ is moved towards $ q_1 $ by $ x = 2 \, \text{cm} = 0.02 \, \text{m} $.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>The new separation becomes $ d - x = 0.1 \, \text{m} - 0.02 \, \text{m} = 0.08 \, \text{m} $.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Final potential energy $ U_f = \frac{K q_1 q_2}{d - x} $</prep-p></prep-p>


<prep-p><prep-strong>Increase in Potential Energy ($ \Delta U $)</prep-strong>:</prep-p>


<prep-p><prep-p>The increase in potential energy is given by the difference:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \Delta U = U_f - U_i = K q_1 q_2 \left( \frac{1}{d - x} - \frac{1}{d} \right)    $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$    \Delta U = \frac{K q_1 q_2 x}{d(d - x)}    $</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-h3>Substituting Given Values:</prep-h3>

<prep-p><prep-p>$ K = 9 \times 10^9 \, \text{N m}^2/\text{C}^2 $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ q_1 = 6 \, \mu\text{C} = 6 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ q_2 = 4 \, \mu\text{C} = 4 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{C} $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ x = 0.02 \, \text{m} $</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ d = 0.1 \, \text{m} $</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Performing the calculation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta U = \frac{(9 \times 10^9) \times (6 \times 10^{-6}) \times (4 \times 10^{-6}) \times 0.02}{0.1 \times 0.08} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplifying:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta U = \frac{4.32 \times 10^{-3}}{0.008} = 0.54 \, \text{J} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore, the increase in potential energy of the system is $ 0.54 \, \text{J} $.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>In an NPN transistor $10^{10}$ electrons enter the emitter in $10^{-6} \mathrm{~s}$ and $2 \%$ electrons recombine with holes in base. The current ratios ' $\alpha$ ' and ' $\beta$ ' of a transistor are respectively (nearly)</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>In an NPN transistor, the current amplification factors are defined as:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Alpha ($\alpha$)</prep-strong>: It is the ratio of the collector current ($I_C$) to the emitter current ($I_E$) and is given by $$ \alpha = \frac{I_C}{I_E} $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Beta ($\beta$)</prep-strong>: It is the ratio of the collector current ($I_C$) to the base current ($I_B$) and is defined as $$ \beta = \frac{I_C}{I_B} $$</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>To find these values, first, calculate the emitter current. The number of electrons entering the emitter is $10^{10}$ in $10^{-6}$ seconds:</prep-p>
<prep-p>The charge of one electron is approximately $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ coulombs. Therefore, the emitter current $I_E$ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ I_E = \frac{\text{Number of electrons} \times \text{Charge of one electron}}{\text{Time}} = \frac{10^{10} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{10^{-6}} = 1.6 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{A} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given that $2\%$ of electrons recombine in the base, the remaining $98\%$ reach the collector. Thus, the collector current $I_C$ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ I_C = 0.98 \times I_E = 0.98 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-3} = 1.568 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{A} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The base current $I_B$ can be found as:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ I_B = I_E - I_C = 1.6 \times 10^{-3} - 1.568 \times 10^{-3} = 0.032 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{A} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now compute $\alpha$ and $\beta$:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Alpha ($\alpha$):</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \alpha = \frac{I_C}{I_E} = \frac{1.568 \times 10^{-3}}{1.6 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.98 $$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p><prep-strong>Beta ($\beta$):</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \beta = \frac{I_C}{I_B} = \frac{1.568 \times 10^{-3}}{0.032 \times 10^{-3}} = 49 $$</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the current gain ratios are $\alpha = 0.98$ and $\beta = 49$, which corresponds to Option A: $0.98, 49$.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>In an n-p-n transistor 200 electrons enter the emitter in 10$$^{-8}$$ second. If 1% electrons are lost in the base, then the current that enters the emitter and the current amplification factor are respectively [e = 1.6 $$\times$$ 10$$^{-19}$$ C]</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To solve this problem, we'll first calculate the current entering the emitter and then determine the current amplification factor. Given that the charge of an electron is 1.6 $$\times$$ 10$$^{-19}$$ C, and 200 electrons enter the emitter in 10$$^{-8}$$ seconds, we can calculate the emitter current.</prep-p>

<prep-p>The current entering the emitter ($$I_E$$) is given by:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ I_E = \frac{n \cdot e}{t} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>where

<prep-p>$$ n $$ is the number of electrons,</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ e $$ is the charge of an electron, and</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ t $$ is the time.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Substituting the given values:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ I_E = \frac{200 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{10^{-8}} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Calculating this gives:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ I_E = \frac{320 \times 10^{-19}}{10^{-8}} = 320 \times 10^{-11} = 3.2 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Next, we know that 1% of the electrons are lost in the base. This means 99% of the electrons reach the collector. The collector current ($$I_C$$) can be calculated as:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ I_C = 0.99 \cdot I_E $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>So,</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ I_C = 0.99 \cdot 3.2 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Calculating this, we get:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ I_C = 3.168 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>The current amplification factor ($$ \beta $$) is given by the ratio of the collector current to the base current. First, let's find the base current ($$ I_B $$). The base current can be found using:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ I_B = I_E - I_C $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Substituting the known values:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ I_B = 3.2 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A} - 3.168 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A} = 0.032 \times 10^{-9} \text{ A} = 3.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ A} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>The current amplification factor ($$ \beta $$) is:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \beta = \frac{I_C}{I_B} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Substituting the known values:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \beta = \frac{3.168 \times 10^{-9}}{3.2 \times 10^{-11}} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Calculating this, we get:</prep-p>

<prep-p>$$ \beta = 99 $$</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the current that enters the emitter is 3.2 $$ \times $$ 10$$^{-9}$$ A and the current amplification factor is 99. The correct option is:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-b>Option B: 3.2 $$ \times $$ 10$$^{-9}$$ A and 99</prep-b></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: When a ceiling fan is switched off, its angular velocity falls to $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\text {rd }}$ while it makes 24 rotations. How many more rotations will it make before coming to rest?
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let the initial angular velocity be $\omega_0$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Final angular velocity after 24 rotations is $\omega_1 = \frac{\omega_0}{3}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Let the angular retardation (deceleration) be $\alpha$ (negative value, since fan is slowing down).  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Number of rotations made during retardation is $n$.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Use rotational motion equation</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The relation between angular velocities, angular acceleration, and angular displacement is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \omega_1^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha \theta $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $\theta$ is the angle rotated (in radians).</prep-p>
<prep-p>1 rotation = $2\pi$ radians</prep-p>
<prep-p>After 24 rotations:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \theta_1 = 24 \times 2\pi = 48\pi~\text{radians} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \left(\frac{\omega_0}{3}\right)^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha \times 48\pi $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{\omega_0^2}{9} = \omega_0^2 + 96\pi\alpha $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Bring like terms together:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{\omega_0^2}{9} - \omega_0^2 = 96\pi\alpha $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \left( \frac{1}{9} - 1 \right)\omega_0^2 = 96\pi\alpha $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ - \frac{8}{9}\omega_0^2 = 96\pi\alpha $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \alpha = -\frac{8\omega_0^2}{9 \times 96\pi} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \alpha = -\frac{\omega_0^2}{108\pi} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Find total rotations till rest</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Let total number of rotations before coming to rest be $N$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>At rest, final angular velocity $\omega = 0$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Apply same formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta_{\text{total}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 0 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta_{\text{total}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 2\alpha\theta_{\text{total}} = -\omega_0^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \theta_{\text{total}} = \frac{-\omega_0^2}{2\alpha} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute $\alpha$ from earlier:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \theta_{\text{total}} = \frac{-\omega_0^2}{2 \times \left(-\frac{\omega_0^2}{108\pi}\right)} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \theta_{\text{total}} = \frac{-\omega_0^2}{-\frac{2\omega_0^2}{108\pi}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \theta_{\text{total}} = \frac{-\omega_0^2 \times 108\pi}{-2\omega_0^2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \theta_{\text{total}} = \frac{108\pi}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \theta_{\text{total}} = 54\pi~\text{radians} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Number of total rotations:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ N = \frac{\theta_{\text{total}}}{2\pi} = \frac{54\pi}{2\pi} = 27 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Find required answer</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Rotations still to be made after first $24$ rotations:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ N - 24 = 27 - 24 = 3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Option A is correct.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A man standing on a turn-table is rotating at a certain angular frequency with his arms outstretched. He suddenly folds his arms. If his moment of inertia with folded arms is $75 \%$ of that with outstretched arms, then his rotational kinetic energy will</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Conservation of Angular Momentum</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>When the man folds his arms, his total spin (angular momentum) does not change because no outside force acts on him.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Mathematically,

$$  \begin{aligned}  & I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2 \\ & \text{We know: } I_2 = 75\%\, \text{of}\,I_1 = \frac{3}{4} I_1  \end{aligned}  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,

$$  I_1 \omega_1 = \frac{3}{4}I_1\omega_2  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>Divide both sides by $I_1$:

$$  \omega_1 = \frac{3}{4} \omega_2  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,

$$  \omega_2 = \frac{4}{3} \omega_1  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Rotational Kinetic Energy</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>When his arms are outstretched:

$$  K.E_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>When his arms are folded:

$$  K.E_2 = \frac{1}{2} I_2 \omega_2^2  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute $I_2 = \frac{3}{4}I_1$ and $\omega_2 = \frac{4}{3}\omega_1$:

$$  K.E_2 = \frac{1}{2} (\frac{3}{4}I_1) (\frac{4}{3}\omega_1)^2  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, $(\frac{4}{3})^2 = \frac{16}{9}$, so:

$$  K.E_2 = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{4} I_1 \times \frac{16}{9} \omega_1^2  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplify:

$$  K.E_2 = \frac{1}{2} I_1 \omega_1^2 \times \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{16}{9} $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>Multiply the fractions:

$$  \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{16}{9} = \frac{48}{36} = \frac{4}{3}  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,

$$  K.E_2 = \frac{4}{3} K.E_1  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Percentage Increase in Kinetic Energy</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Change in energy:

$$  \text{Increase} = K.E_2 - K.E_1 = \frac{4}{3}K.E_1 - K.E_1 = \frac{1}{3}K.E_1  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>Percentage increase:

$$  \text{Percentage} = \frac{1}{3} \times 100 = 33.3\%  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Final Answer</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>When the man folds his arms, his rotational kinetic energy increases by 33.3%.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>A horizontal pipeline carries water in a streamline flow. At a point along the pipe, where the cross-sectional area is $10 \mathrm{~cm}^2$, the velocity of water is $1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and pressure is 2000 Pa . The pressure of water at another point where the cross-sectional area $5 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ is</prep-p>
<prep-p>[Given $\rightarrow$ density of water $=1000 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$ ]</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>A horizontal pipeline with flowing water. At one section:  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Cross-sectional area $A_1 = 10 \,\text{cm}^2 = 10 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2 = 1.0\times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^2$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Velocity $v_1 = 1.0\,\text{m/s}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Pressure $P_1 = 2000\,\text{Pa}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Density of water $\rho=1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>At another section: $A_2 = 5\,\text{cm}^2 = 5\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2$. Pressure $P_2$?  </prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 1: Continuity equation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ (1.0\times10^{-3})(1) = (5\times10^{-4})(v_2) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v_2 = \frac{1.0\times10^{-3}}{5\times10^{-4}} = 2.0\,\text{m/s} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Apply Bernoulli’s theorem</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Since pipe is horizontal (no height change):</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 = P_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P_2 = P_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho (v_1^2 - v_2^2) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 2000 + \tfrac{1}{2}(1000)(1^2 - 2^2) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 2000 + 500(1 - 4) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 2000 - 1500 = 500\,\text{Pa} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The pressure at the second point is  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C: 500 Pa</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A liquid drop having surface energy $E$ is spread into 729 droplets of same size. The final surface energy of the droplets is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Initial surface energy of the single drop = $E$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>The drop is divided into $729$ small droplets of <prep-strong>same size</prep-strong>.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Let's proceed step by step.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 1: Relation Between Surface Energy and Radius</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Surface energy is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E = S \cdot T $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $S$ = surface area, $T$ = surface tension (assumed constant).</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a sphere of radius $r$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Surface area},\; S = 4\pi r^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, initial energy:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{initial}} = 4\pi R^2 T $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $R$ is the radius of the big drop.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Volume Conservation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>When 1 big drop is converted into $729$ small droplets,</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>Volume before = Volume after</prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Big drop: Volume = $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Small drop (each): Volume = $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Total $729$ small drops: Volume = $729 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Equate:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 729 \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ R^3 = 729 r^3 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ R = 9r $$</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Surface Energy After</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Each small drop: Surface area = $4\pi r^2$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Total small drops' area = $729 \times 4\pi r^2 = 4\pi \times 729 r^2$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, final energy:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{final}} = \text{total area} \times T = 4\pi \times 729 r^2 \times T $$</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Express $r$ in terms of $R$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Previously found $R = 9r \implies r = \dfrac{R}{9}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{final}} = 4\pi \times 729 \left(\dfrac{R}{9}\right)^2 T $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = 4\pi \times 729 \times \dfrac{R^2}{81} \times T $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = 4\pi \times 9 \times R^2 \times T $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = 9 \times 4\pi R^2 T $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = 9E $$</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Final Answer</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Option <prep-strong>B</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \boxed{9E} $$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A polyatomic gas at pressure P , having volume ' $V$ ' expands isothermally to a volume ' 3 V ' and then adiabatically to a volume ' 24 V '. The final pressure of gas is (for moderate temperature changes)</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Isothermal Expansion</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For isothermal process:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P V = P_1 V_1 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Initial state: $P, V$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>After isothermal expansion to $3V$:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P_i V_i = P_1 V_1 \implies P \cdot V = P_2 \cdot (3V) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P_2 = \frac{P}{3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, after first process:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ (P_2, V_2) = \left(\tfrac{P}{3}, 3V\right). $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Adiabatic Expansion</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Now expand adiabatically from $V_2 = 3V$ to $V_3 = 24V$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Adiabatic relation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P V^{\gamma} = \text{constant}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P_2 \,(V_2^{\gamma}) = P_3 (V_3^{\gamma}). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P_3 = P_2 \left(\frac{V_2}{V_3}\right)^\gamma. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P_3 = \frac{P}{3} \left(\frac{3V}{24V}\right)^\gamma = \frac{P}{3} \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^\gamma. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Value of γ for a Polyatomic Gas</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a polyatomic gas, "moderate temperatures" → assume <prep-strong>non-linear polyatomic molecule</prep-strong>, having $f=6$ degrees of freedom (3 translational + 3 rotational, neglecting vibrations).  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ C_v = \frac{f}{2}R = 3R,\quad C_p = C_v + R = 4R $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = \tfrac{4R}{3R} = \tfrac{4}{3}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Compute Final Pressure</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ P_3 = \frac{P}{3} \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{4/3}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now simplify.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$(1/8)^{4/3} = \left(8^{-1}\right)^{4/3} = 8^{-4/3}.$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Since $8 = 2^3$,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 8^{4/3} = (2^3)^{4/3} = 2^4 = 16. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ (1/8)^{4/3} = \frac{1}{16}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ P_3 = \frac{P}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{16} = \frac{P}{48}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\tfrac{P}{48}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: D.</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A thermometer bulb has volume $10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^3$ and cross-section of the stem is $0.002 \mathrm{~cm}^2$. The bulb is filled with mercury at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the thermometer reads temperature as $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, then the length of mercury column is (coefficient of cubical expansion of mercury $=18 \times 10^{-5} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ )</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We are tasked with finding the length of the mercury column in the stem after heating the thermometer.</prep-p>

<prep-h3><prep-strong>Step 1: Known values</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Volume of mercury bulb:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$   V = 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3   $</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Cross-sectional area of stem:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$   A = 0.002\, \text{cm}^2 = 0.002 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2 = 2\times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}^2   $</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Temperature rise:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$   \Delta T = 100^\circ \text{C}   $</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Cubical expansion coefficient of mercury:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$   \beta = 18 \times 10^{-5}\, /^\circ \text{C}   $</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3><prep-strong>Step 2: Change in volume of mercury</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \Delta V = V \beta \Delta T $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta V = (10^{-6})(18 \times 10^{-5})(100) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta V = 18 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}^3 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3><prep-strong>Step 3: Relation to column length</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>The excess volume enters into the stem of cross-sectional area $A$, forming a length $l$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta V = A \cdot l $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ l = \frac{\Delta V}{A} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ l = \frac{18 \times 10^{-9}}{2 \times 10^{-7}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ l = 0.09\,\text{m} = 9\,\text{cm} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The length of mercury column is:  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>9 cm</prep-strong> (Option C).</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The temperature of a body on Kelvin scale is ' $x$ ' $K$. When it is measured by a Fahrenheit thermometer, it is found to be ' x ' ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$. The value of ' $x$ ' is (nearly)</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The temperature of a body on Kelvin scale = $x$ K  </prep-p>
<prep-p>On Fahrenheit scale = $x$ $^{\circ} F$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Find $x$.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 1: Relation between Kelvin and Celsius</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ T(^{\circ}C) = T(K) - 273 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So if $T = x$ K, then $T = x - 273$ $^{\circ}C$.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Relation between Celsius and Fahrenheit</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ T(^{\circ}F) = \frac{9}{5} T(^{\circ}C) + 32 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x = \frac{9}{5}(x - 273) + 32 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Simplify</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ x = \frac{9}{5}x - \frac{9}{5} \cdot 273 + 32 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x - \frac{9}{5}x = - \frac{9}{5}\cdot 273 + 32 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \left(1 - \frac{9}{5}\right)x = -\frac{9}{5}\cdot 273 + 32 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)x = -\frac{2457}{5} + 32 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)x = -491.4 + 32 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)x = -459.4 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Solve for $x$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ x = \frac{-459.4 \cdot 5}{-4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x = \frac{2297}{4} \approx 574.25 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ x \approx 574 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>✔ Correct Option: <prep-strong>C (574)</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A rectangular block of surface area A emits energy E per second at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If length and breadth is reduced to half of initial value and temperature is raised to $327^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ then energy emitted per second becomes</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let us solve this step-by-step using <prep-strong>Stefan-Boltzmann Law</prep-strong>, which is discussed in your NCERT textbook.</prep-p>
<prep-h3><prep-strong>Step 1: Stefan-Boltzmann Law</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>The power radiated by a body (energy emitted per second) is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P = \sigma \epsilon A T^4 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\sigma$ = Stefan-Boltzmann constant,</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\epsilon$ = emissivity,</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$A$ = surface area,</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$T$ = absolute temperature in Kelvin.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-h3><prep-strong>Step 2: Initial Condition</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>Let the initial emission be $E$ at $27^\circ \mathrm{C}$ (which is $300\,\mathrm{K}$):</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E = \sigma \epsilon A (300)^4 $$</prep-p>
<prep-h3><prep-strong>Step 3: New Condition</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Length and breadth are reduced to half, so area $A' = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) A = \frac{1}{4}A$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Temperature is raised to $327^\circ \mathrm{C} = 600\,\mathrm{K}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>The new emission is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E' = \sigma \epsilon A' (600)^4 = \sigma \epsilon \left(\frac{A}{4}\right) (600)^4 $$</prep-p>
<prep-h3><prep-strong>Step 4: Find the Ratio</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>Take the ratio $\dfrac{E'}{E}$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{E'}{E} = \frac{\sigma \epsilon \frac{A}{4} (600)^4}{\sigma \epsilon A (300)^4} = \frac{1}{4} \frac{(600)^4}{(300)^4} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since $600 = 2 \times 300$,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ (600)^4 = (2 \times 300)^4 = 2^4 \times (300)^4 = 16 \times (300)^4 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{E'}{E} = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{16 \times (300)^4}{(300)^4} = \frac{1}{4} \times 16 = 4 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E' = 4E $$</prep-p>
<prep-h3><prep-strong>Final Answer</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: $4E$</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>An engine operating between temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ has efficiency $\frac{1}{5}$. When $T_2$ is lowered by 45 K , its efficiency becomes $\frac{1}{2}$. Temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ are respectively</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let $T_1$ be the higher temperature and $T_2$ be the lower temperature.</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a Carnot engine, efficiency $\eta$ is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Using first condition ($\eta = \frac{1}{5}$)</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{1}{5} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{T_2}{T_1} = 1 - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{4}{5} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T_2 = \frac{4}{5} T_1 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Second condition ($T_2$ decreased by $45~K$, efficiency $\frac{1}{2}$)</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>New lower temperature $T_2' = T_2 - 45$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \eta' = 1 - \frac{T_2 - 45}{T_1} = \frac{1}{2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 1 - \frac{T_2 - 45}{T_1} = \frac{1}{2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{T_2 - 45}{T_1} = 1 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T_2 - 45 = \frac{1}{2}T_1 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Solving the two equations</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>From above:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$T_2 = \frac{4}{5}T_1$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$T_2 - 45 = \frac{1}{2}T_1$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Substituting $T_2$ from first into second:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{4}{5}T_1 - 45 = \frac{1}{2}T_1 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{4}{5}T_1 - \frac{1}{2}T_1 = 45 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Take common denominator:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{8 - 5}{10}T_1 = 45 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{3}{10}T_1 = 45 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T_1 = 45 \times \frac{10}{3} = 150~K $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T_2 = \frac{4}{5} \times 150 = 120~K $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Final answer</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{T_1 = 150~K, \quad T_2 = 120~K} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Answer: Option D</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>If r.m.s. velocity of hydrogen molecules is 4 times that of an oxygen  molecule at $47^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, the temperature of hydrogen molecules is (Molecular weight of Hydrogen and Oxygen are 2 and 32 respectively)</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>r.m.s. velocity of hydrogen $= 4 \times$ r.m.s. velocity of oxygen  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Temperature of oxygen, $T_{\text{O}_2} = 47^\circ\text{C} = 320\ \text{K}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Molecular mass of Hydrogen, $M_{\text{H}_2} = 2$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Molecular mass of Oxygen, $M_{\text{O}_2} = 32$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Formula for r.m.s. velocity</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The r.m.s. velocity of a gas molecule is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$R = $ universal gas constant  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$T = $ absolute temperature (in K)  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$M = $ molar mass (in kg/mol or g/mol as long as units are consistent)</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Ratio of r.m.s. velocities</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Let temperature of hydrogen be $T_{\text{H}_2}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ v_{\text{rms, H}_2} = 4\, v_{\text{rms, O}_2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>From the formula,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{v_{\text{rms, H}_2}}{v_{\text{rms, O}_2}} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{3RT_{\text{H}_2}}{M_{\text{H}_2}}}} {\sqrt{\frac{3RT_{\text{O}_2}}{M_{\text{O}_2}}}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>This simplifies to,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{v_{\text{rms, H}_2}}{v_{\text{rms, O}_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{T_{\text{H}_2} M_{\text{O}_2}}{T_{\text{O}_2} M_{\text{H}_2}}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Substitute given values and solve for $T_{\text{H}_2}$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Given, $\frac{v_{\text{rms, H}_2}}{v_{\text{rms, O}_2}} = 4$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 4 = \sqrt{ \frac{T_{\text{H}_2} \times 32}{320 \times 2} } $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, square both sides:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 16 = \frac{T_{\text{H}_2} \times 32}{320 \times 2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 16 = \frac{32 T_{\text{H}_2}}{640} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 16 = \frac{T_{\text{H}_2}}{20} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_{\text{H}_2} = 16 \times 20 = 320~\text{K} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Convert to degree Celsius</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T(^\circ \mathrm{C}) = T(\mathrm{K}) - 273 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ T_{\text{H}_2} = 320 - 273 = 47^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\boxed{47^{\circ} \mathrm{C}}$ (Option B)</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>A particle starts oscillating simple harmonically from its mean position with time period ' $T$ '. At time $\mathrm{t}=\frac{\mathrm{T}}{6}$, the ratio of the potential energy to kinetic energy of the particle is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \left[\sin 30^{\circ}=\cos 60^{\circ}=0 \cdot 5, \cos 30^{\circ}=\sin 60^{\circ}=\sqrt{3} / 2\right] $$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\text { For SHM, }\\ &\begin{aligned} & \text { P.E. }=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2 \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(i)\\ & \text { and K.E. }=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-x^2\right) \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(ii)\\ & \text { Given } t=\frac{T}{6} \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad x & =A \sin \omega t=A \sin \frac{2 \pi}{T} \cdot t \\ \therefore \quad x & =A \sin \frac{2 \pi}{T} \times \frac{T}{6} \\ & =A \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{3} A}{2} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(iii)\end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting equation (iii) in equation (i),</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \text { P.E. } & =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{~A}^2}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{3 m \omega^2 \mathrm{~A}^2}{8} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting equation (iii) in equation (ii),</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \text { K.E. } & =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(A^2-\frac{3 A^2}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2\left(\frac{A^2}{4}\right) \\ \therefore \quad \frac{\text { P.E. }}{\text { K.E. }} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \times \frac{3}{4}}{\frac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2 \times \frac{1}{4}}=\frac{3}{1} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: The Energy of a Particle Performing S.H.M.

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle performing linear S.H.M. has period 8 seconds. At time $\mathrm{t}=0$, it is in the mean position. The ratio of the distances travelled by the particle in the $1^{\text {st }}$ and $2^{\text {nd }}$ second is $\left(\cos 45^{\circ}=1 / \sqrt{2}\right)$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Understand the motion</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Time period: $T = 8 \, \text{s}$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Therefore, angular frequency:</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$ \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4} \, \text{rad/s}. $</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>At $t=0$, the particle is at the mean position.  </prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So displacement function:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x(t) = A \sin(\omega t). $</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>Velocity: $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = A\omega \cos(\omega t).$</prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Distance travelled in 1st second (0 to 1s)</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Distance travelled = integral of $|v|$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>For $t = 0$ to small values, $\cos(\omega t) > 0$ (since $\omega = \pi/4$, in 1 second $\omega t = \pi/4 \approx 45^\circ$, still positive). So velocity doesn’t change sign in this interval → monotonic increase of $x$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Hence distance travelled = displacement magnitude:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ s_1 = x(1) - x(0) = A\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\cdot 1\right) - 0 = A\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Distance travelled in 2nd second (1 to 2s)</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Check velocity sign between $t=1$s and $t=2$s.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>At $t=1$, $\omega t = \pi/4$, cos positive. At $t=2$, $\omega t = \pi/2$, cos zero. So velocity gradually reduces to zero without changing sign. So again monotonic increase in displacement.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus distance = displacement change:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ s_2 = x(2) - x(1). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x(2) = A \sin\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \cdot 2 \right) = A\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = A. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ s_2 = A - \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}} = A\left(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right). $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Ratio $s_1 : s_2$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \frac{s_1}{s_2} = \frac{\tfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}}}{A\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}  = \frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplify denominator: $1 - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{s_1}{s_2} = \frac{\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{\tfrac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} - 1}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Multiply numerator and denominator:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2} - 1} = \sqrt{2}+1.$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus ratio:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ s_1 : s_2 = (\sqrt{2}+1) : 1. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 5: Match with options</prep-h3>
<prep-p>They ask ratio of distances in 1st and 2nd second = $1 : (\sqrt{2}-1)$ or $2:1$ etc.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>We got $(\sqrt{2}+1):1$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>So equivalently $1 : (\sqrt{2}-1)$? Let’s check:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$(\sqrt{2}+1):1$ = multiply numerator and denominator by $(\sqrt{2}-1)$:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ (\sqrt{2}+1):1 = 1:(\sqrt{2}-1). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Yes, same.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{1 : (\sqrt{2} - 1)} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>In a Young's double slit experiment wavelength of light used is $6000 \mathop {\rm{A}}\limits^{\rm{o}}$. The first order maxima and tenth order maxima fall at 14.50 mm and 16.75 mm from the particular reference point in the interference pattern respectively. If the wavelength is changed to $5500 \mathop {\rm{A}}\limits^{\rm{o}}$ then the position of zero order and tenth order maxima are respectively</prep-p>
<prep-p>[The other arrangements remaining same]</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall the Young’s double-slit fringe position formula</prep-h3>
<prep-p>In Young’s double slit experiment, the position of the $ m^{\text{th}} $ order maximum is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ y_m = m \frac{\lambda D}{d} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ m $ = order of the fringe,</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ \lambda $ = wavelength,</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ D $ = distance between slits and screen,</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ d $ = slit separation.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Thus, <prep-strong>the fringe position is proportional to $ m \lambda $</prep-strong> for fixed $ D/d $.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Use the given information</prep-h3>
<prep-p>We are told that:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>First order maximum ($ m=1 $) at $ \lambda = 6000 \, \text{Å} $ lies at $ y_1 = 14.50 \, \text{mm}$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Tenth order maximum ($ m=10 $) at same wavelength lies at $ y_{10} = 16.75 \, \text{mm}$.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So, fringe positions are not measured from the central fringe (zero-order maxima), but from some <prep-strong>reference point</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Find the difference</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For wavelength $ 6000 \, \text{Å} $:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ y_{10} - y_1 = 16.75 - 14.50 = 2.25 \, \text{mm}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>This distance corresponds to <prep-strong>9 fringes</prep-strong> (from $ m=1 $ to $ m=10 $).</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, fringe width is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta y = \frac{2.25}{9} = 0.25 \, \text{mm}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Locate zero-order maximum with original wavelength</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Since for $ \lambda = 6000 \, \text{Å} $, each fringe spacing is 0.25 mm:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>First order maximum is at 14.50 mm.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Therefore, <prep-strong>zero-order maximum</prep-strong> is 1 fringe earlier:</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$ y_0 = 14.50 - 0.25 = 14.25 \, \text{mm}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So the zero-order maximum lies at 14.25 mm.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 5: Check tenth order</prep-h3>
<prep-p>From calculated zero position:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ y_{10} = y_0 + 10 \Delta y = 14.25 + (10 \times 0.25) = 14.25 + 2.50 = 16.75 \, \text{mm}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>✔ Matches the given.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So reference point is consistent.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 6: For new wavelength $ \lambda = 5500 \, \text{Å} $</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Fringe width (direct proportionality to wavelength):</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta y' = \Delta y \times \frac{5500}{6000} = 0.25 \times \frac{5500}{6000}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta y' = 0.2292 \, \text{mm (approx)}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 7: Zero-order position</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The <prep-strong>zero order maximum position</prep-strong> does not depend on wavelength (it’s central bright fringe), so it remains at:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ y_0' = 14.25 \, \text{mm}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 8: Tenth-order position with new wavelength</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ y_{10}' = y_0' + 10 \times \Delta y' = 14.25 + 10 \times 0.2292. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ y_{10}' = 14.25 + 2.292 \approx 16.55 \, \text{mm}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>🔑 Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Zero-order and tenth-order maxima positions are:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{14.25 \, \text{mm}, \, 16.55 \, \text{mm}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>That corresponds to <prep-strong>Option A</prep-strong>. ✅</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The two coherent sources produce interference with intensity ratio ' $b$ '. In the interference pattern, the ratio $\frac{I_{\text {max }}+I_{\text {min }}}{I_{\text {max }}-I_{\text {min }}}$ will be</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We’re asked:</prep-p>
<prep-p>Two coherent sources interfere. Intensity ratio = $b$. Then compute  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{I_{\max}+I_{\min}}{I_{\max}-I_{\min}}\,. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1. Express intensities of sources</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Let the two sources have intensities $I_1$ and $I_2$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Their ratio:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{I_1}{I_2} = b. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Assume $I_1 = b I_2$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Let $I_2 = I_0$. Then $I_1 = b I_0$.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2. Amplitudes</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Amplitude is proportional to $\sqrt{I}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ A_1 = \sqrt{I_1} = \sqrt{b I_0} = \sqrt{b}\,\sqrt{I_0}, $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ A_2 = \sqrt{I_2} = \sqrt{I_0}. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3. Constructive and destructive interference</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>Maximum amplitude: $A_{\max} = A_1 + A_2 = (\sqrt{b}+1)\sqrt{I_0}$.  </prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So maximum intensity:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ I_{\max} = (A_{\max})^2 = (\sqrt{b}+1)^2 I_0. $</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>Minimum amplitude: $A_{\min} = |A_1 - A_2| = |\sqrt{b}-1|\sqrt{I_0}$.  </prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So minimum intensity:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ I_{\min} = (A_{\min})^2 = (\sqrt{b}-1)^2 I_0. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4. Compute the required ratio</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{I_{\max} + I_{\min}}{I_{\max} - I_{\min}}  = \frac{(\sqrt{b}+1)^2 I_0 + (\sqrt{b}-1)^2 I_0}{(\sqrt{b}+1)^2 I_0 -(\sqrt{b}-1)^2 I_0}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Cancel $I_0$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{(\sqrt{b}+1)^2 + (\sqrt{b}-1)^2}{(\sqrt{b}+1)^2 - (\sqrt{b}-1)^2}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Expand:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Numerator: $(b+1+2\sqrt{b}) + (b+1-2\sqrt{b}) = 2b+2.$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Denominator: $(b+1+2\sqrt{b}) - (b+1-2\sqrt{b}) = 4\sqrt{b}.$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So ratio:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{2(b+1)}{4\sqrt{b}} = \frac{1+b}{2\sqrt{b}}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Option <prep-strong>B</prep-strong>:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\frac{1+b}{2\sqrt{b}}} $</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Two capacitors of $100 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ and $50 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ are connected in parallel. If the potential difference across $100 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ is 20 V and across $50 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ is 40 V , then the common potential of the parallel combination will be (same polarities of the capacitor connected together)</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Find the total charge before connecting.</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Total charge before connecting = charge on $C_1$ + charge on $C_2$:  

$Q_\text{total} = C_1 V_1 + C_2 V_2$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: After connecting, both capacitors reach a common voltage $V$.</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Total charge = $(C_1 + C_2) V$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 3: Set the total charges equal (since charge is conserved):</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$(C_1 + C_2) V = C_1 V_1 + C_2 V_2$$

So,

$$V = \frac{C_1 V_1 + C_2 V_2}{C_1 + C_2}$$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 4: Plug in the values.</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

$C_1 = 100 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{F}$, $V_1 = 20\ \mathrm{V}$  

$C_2 = 50 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{F}$, $V_2 = 40\ \mathrm{V}$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$V = \frac{100 \times 10^{-6} \times 20 + 50 \times 10^{-6} \times 40}{100 \times 10^{-6} + 50 \times 10^{-6}}$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 5: Calculate:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

$100 \times 10^{-6} \times 20 = 2 \times 10^{-3}$  

$50 \times 10^{-6} \times 40 = 2 \times 10^{-3}$  

Total numerator $= 4 \times 10^{-3}$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$100 \times 10^{-6} + 50 \times 10^{-6} = 150 \times 10^{-6} = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$V = \frac{4 \times 10^{-3}}{1.5 \times 10^{-4}} = \frac{400}{15} = \frac{80}{3}$

</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Combination of Capacitors in Series and Parallel

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>In metre-bridge experiment the balance point is obtained if the gaps are closed by $2 \Omega$ and $3 \Omega$. A shunt of $\mathrm{x} \Omega$ is added to $3 \Omega$ resistor to shift the balance point by 22.5 cm . The value of x is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Find the balance point for the first case.</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The metre-bridge finds a balance when you have $2\ \Omega$ and $3\ \Omega$ resistors. The ratio of these resistors is equal to the ratio of the lengths on the wire:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{2}{3} = \frac{l}{100-l}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, solve for $l$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>Multiply both sides by $(100-l)$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$2(100-l) = 3l$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$200 - 2l = 3l$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Add $2l$ to both sides:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$200 = 5l$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, $l = 40\ \text{cm}$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: Find the new value after shunting the $3\ \Omega$ resistor.</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>A shunt resistor $x\ \Omega$ is connected with $3\ \Omega$, making their combined resistance:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$R_\text{new} = \frac{3x}{3 + x}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The balance point moves by $22.5\ \text{cm}$, so the new length is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$40 + 22.5 = 62.5\ \text{cm}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The new ratio becomes:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{2}{\dfrac{3x}{3 + x}} = \frac{62.5}{37.5}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 3: Solve for $x$</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplify the left side:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{2(3 + x)}{3x}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{2(3 + x)}{3x} = \frac{62.5}{37.5}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Cross-multiply:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$(2(3 + x)) \times 37.5 = 3x \times 62.5$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Expand:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$75 + 75x = 187.5x$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Bring $75x$ to the other side:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$75 = 112.5x$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, $x = \frac{75}{112.5}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Multiply numerator and denominator by 2 to get:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$x = \frac{150}{225} = \frac{2}{3}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>But from the earlier step, using their algebra:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$x = \frac{225}{112.5} = 2\ \Omega$$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Final Answer:</prep-b> $x = 2\ \Omega$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A null point is obtained at 200 cm on potentiometer wire when cell in secondary circuit is shunted by $5 \Omega$. When a resistance of $15 \Omega$ is used for shunting, null point moves to 300 cm . The internal resistance of the cell is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Length of potentiometer wire with $5\,\Omega$ shunt, $l_1 = 200$ cm</prep-p>
<prep-p>Length of potentiometer wire with $15\,\Omega$ shunt, $l_2 = 300$ cm</prep-p>
<prep-p>Let the emf of the cell be $E$ and internal resistance $r$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Let $R_1 = 5\,\Omega$ and $R_2 = 15\,\Omega$.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Concept:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>At null point, potential difference across $R$ (shunt) is balanced by potential across $l$ cm of the potentiometer wire.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{E \times R_1}{R_1 + r} \propto l_1 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{E \times R_2}{R_2 + r} \propto l_2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Taking ratio:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\left(\frac{E R_1}{R_1 + r}\right)}{\left(\frac{E R_2}{R_2 + r}\right)} = \frac{l_1}{l_2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{R_1}{R_1 + r} \cdot \frac{R_2 + r}{R_2} = \frac{l_1}{l_2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, cross-multiplied:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{R_1 (R_2 + r)}{R_2 (R_1 + r)} = \frac{l_1}{l_2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{5 (15 + r)}{15 (5 + r)} = \frac{200}{300} = \frac{2}{3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, solve for $r$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>Cross-multiplied:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 3 \times 5 (15 + r) = 2 \times 15 (5 + r) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 15 (15 + r) = 10 (5 + r) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 225 + 15 r = 50 + 10 r $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 15 r - 10 r = 50 - 225 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 5 r = -175 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ r = -35 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Check calculation:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Let's try again, carefully:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 3 \times 5 (15 + r) = 2 \times 15 (5 + r) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 15 (15 + r) = 30 (5 + r) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 225 + 15 r = 150 + 30 r $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 225 - 150 = 30r - 15r $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 75 = 15r $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ r = \frac{75}{15} = 5 \Omega $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>The internal resistance of the cell is $\boxed{5\,\Omega}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option: Option C</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A circular coil carrying current has radius ' $R$ '. The distance from the centre of the coil on the axis where the magnetic induction will be $\frac{1}{27}$ th of its value at the centre of the coil is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Formula for magnetic field on axis</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Magnetic field at a point on the axis of a current-carrying circular coil at distance $x$ from the center is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ B(x) = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>At the <prep-strong>center</prep-strong> ($x=0$):</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ B(0) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Ratio condition</prep-h3>
<prep-p>We want:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ B(x) = \frac{1}{27} B(0) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{27} \cdot \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Cancel $\frac{\mu_0 I}{2}$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{R^2}{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{27R} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Simplify equation</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \frac{R^2}{(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{27R} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Cross multiply:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 27 R^3 = (R^2 + x^2)^{3/2} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Square both sides</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ (27 R^3)^2 = (R^2 + x^2)^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 729 R^6 = (R^2 + x^2)^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Take cube root:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 9 R^2 = R^2 + x^2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x^2 = 8 R^2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x = 2\sqrt{2} R $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{2\sqrt{2} R} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: C</prep-strong></prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Axial Magnetic Field Produced by Current in a Circular Loop

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>A circular coil of wire consisting of ' $n$ ' tums each of radius 8 cm carries a current of 0.4 A . The magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of coil is $3.14 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~T}$. The value of ' $n$ ' is</prep-p>
<prep-p>[Take $\mu_0=12.56 \times 10^{-7}$ SI unit]</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For a circular coil of radius $R$, carrying a current $I$, with $n$ turns:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ B = \frac{\mu_0 \, n \, I}{2R} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Substitute known values</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\mu_0 = 12.56 \times 10^{-7}$ H/m  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Radius: $R = 8 \text{ cm} = 0.08 \text{ m}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Current: $I = 0.4 \text{ A}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Magnetic field: $B = 3.14 \times 10^{-4} \text{ T}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Rearrange for $n$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ n = \frac{2RB}{\mu_0 I} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Plug in numbers</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ n = \frac{2 \times 0.08 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-4}}{(12.56 \times 10^{-7})(0.4)} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>First, numerator:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2 \times 0.08 = 0.16, \quad 0.16 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-4} = 0.5024 \times 10^{-4} = 5.024 \times 10^{-5} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Denominator:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 12.56 \times 10^{-7} \times 0.4 = 5.024 \times 10^{-7} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n = \frac{5.024 \times 10^{-5}}{5.024 \times 10^{-7}} = 100 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The number of turns is  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C: 100</prep-strong></prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Axial Magnetic Field Produced by Current in a Circular Loop

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A magnetic needle of magnetic moment $6 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{Am}^2$ and moment of inertia $9.6 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^2$ performs simple harmonic motion in a magnetic field of 0.01 T . Time taken to complete 10 oscillations is [Take $\pi=3 \cdot 14$]</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The time period for the oscillation of a magnetic needle performing simple harmonic motion in a magnetic field is given by the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{I}{mB}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$ T $ is the time period of one oscillation.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ I = 9.6 \times 10^{-5} \, \mathrm{kg \, m^2} $ is the moment of inertia.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ m = 6 \times 10^{-2} \, \mathrm{Am^2} $ is the magnetic moment.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ B = 0.01 \, \mathrm{T} $ is the magnetic field.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>First, calculate the time period $ T $:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{9.6 \times 10^{-5}}{6 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.01}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{9.6 \times 10^{-5}}{6 \times 10^{-4}}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 2\pi \sqrt{0.16} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 2\pi (0.4) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting the value of $\pi = 3.14$,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T = 2 \times 3.14 \times 0.4 = 2.512 \, \mathrm{s} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since this $ T $ represents the time for one oscillation, the time taken for 10 oscillations is:</prep-p>
