<prep-p>$ 10T = 10 \times 2.512 \, \mathrm{s} = 25.12 \, \mathrm{s} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>The correct answer is thus:</prep-p>
<prep-p>Option C: 25.12 s</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Torque Acting on a Magnetic Dipole in a Uniform Magnetic Field

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A coil of effective area $3 \mathrm{~m}^2$ is placed at right angles to a magnetic field of induction $0.05 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2$ If the field is decreased to $20 \%$ of its original value in 10 second, the e.m.f. induced in the coil will be</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-ol>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Identify the given values:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Effective Area (A) = $3 \mathrm{~m}^2$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Initial Magnetic Field Induction ($B_1$) = $0.05 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Final Magnetic Field Induction ($B_2$) = $20\%$ of $B_1 = 0.20 \times 0.05 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2 = 0.01 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Time taken for the change ($\Delta t$) = $10 \mathrm{~s}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>The coil is placed at right angles to the magnetic field, meaning the angle between the normal to the coil's area and the magnetic field is $0^\circ$. So, $\cos\theta = \cos 0^\circ = 1$.</prep-p></prep-li></prep-ul></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Calculate the initial magnetic flux ($\Phi_1$):</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Magnetic flux ($\Phi$) = $B \times A \times \cos\theta$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Phi_1 = B_1 \times A \times 1$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Phi_1 = 0.05 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2 \times 3 \mathrm{~m}^2$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Phi_1 = 0.15 \mathrm{~Wb}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Calculate the final magnetic flux ($\Phi_2$):</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Phi_2 = B_2 \times A \times 1$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Phi_2 = 0.01 \mathrm{~Wb} / \mathrm{m}^2 \times 3 \mathrm{~m}^2$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Phi_2 = 0.03 \mathrm{~Wb}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Calculate the change in magnetic flux ($\Delta\Phi$):</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Delta\Phi = \Phi_2 - \Phi_1$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Delta\Phi = 0.03 \mathrm{~Wb} - 0.15 \mathrm{~Wb}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\Delta\Phi = -0.12 \mathrm{~Wb}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Apply Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The induced e.m.f. ($\varepsilon$) is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\varepsilon = -N \frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Assuming $N=1$ (single turn coil, as not specified otherwise):</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\varepsilon = - \frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\varepsilon = - \frac{-0.12 \mathrm{~Wb}}{10 \mathrm{~s}}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\varepsilon = \frac{0.12}{10} \mathrm{~V}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\varepsilon = 0.012 \mathrm{~V}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Convert the e.m.f. to millivolts (mV):</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$1 \mathrm{~V} = 1000 \mathrm{~mV}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\varepsilon = 0.012 \mathrm{~V} \times 1000 \mathrm{~mV/V}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\varepsilon = 12 \mathrm{~mV}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ol>
<prep-p>The induced e.m.f. in the coil will be $12 \mathrm{~mV}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>The final answer is $\boxed{\text{12 mV}}$.</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Induced Emf in a Stationary Coil in a Changing Magnetic Field

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The magnetic flux through a coil is $4 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~Wb}$ at time $t=0$. It reduces to $30 \%$ of its original value in time $t$ second. If e.m.f. induced in the coil is 0.56 mV then the value of $t$ is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Initial flux, $\phi_1 = 4 \times 10^{-4}~\text{Wb}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Final flux, $\phi_2 = 30\%$ of $\phi_1 = 0.3 \times 4 \times 10^{-4} = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}~\text{Wb}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Induced emf, $e = 0.56~\text{mV} = 0.56 \times 10^{-3}~\text{V}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Time interval, $t = ?$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Formula for average induced emf</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ e = \frac{\left|\phi_2 - \phi_1\right|}{t} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Substituting the values</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ e = \frac{\left|1.2 \times 10^{-4} - 4 \times 10^{-4}\right|}{t} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ e = \frac{\left|-2.8 \times 10^{-4}\right|}{t} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ e = \frac{2.8 \times 10^{-4}}{t} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given $e = 0.56 \times 10^{-3}~\text{V} = 5.6 \times 10^{-4}~\text{V}$ (But $0.56~\text{mV}$ is $0.56 \times 10^{-3}$, or $5.6 \times 10^{-4}$ — check carefully.)</prep-p>
<prep-p>But $0.56~\text{mV} = 0.56 \times 10^{-3} = 5.6 \times 10^{-4}~\text{V}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 5.6 \times 10^{-4} = \frac{2.8 \times 10^{-4}}{t} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Solve for $t$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 5.6 \times 10^{-4} \cdot t = 2.8 \times 10^{-4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ t = \frac{2.8 \times 10^{-4}}{5.6 \times 10^{-4}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ t = \frac{2.8}{5.6} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ t = 0.5~\text{s} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A: $0.5~\text{s}$</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>In an $L-R$ circuit, the inductive reactance is equal to $\sqrt{3}$ times the resistance ' $R$ ' of the circuit. An e.1n.f. $\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{E}_0 \sin (\omega \mathrm{t})$ is applied to the circuit. The power consumed in the circuit is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Inductive reactance, $X_L = \sqrt{3} R$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Applied emf, $E = E_0 \sin(\omega t)$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Let’s proceed step by step:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>1. Impedance of the Circuit</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The total impedance ($Z$) of an $L-R$ circuit is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given $X_L = \sqrt{3} R$, so:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (\sqrt{3}R)^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + 3R^2} = \sqrt{4R^2} = 2R $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>2. Expression for rms values</prep-strong> </prep-p>
<prep-p>The root mean square (rms) value of the applied emf:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{rms}} = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The rms current in the circuit:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{E_{\text{rms}}}{Z} = \frac{E_0/\sqrt{2}}{2R} = \frac{E_0}{2R\sqrt{2}} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>3. Power Consumed</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The average power consumed is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P = E_{\text{rms}} \cdot I_{\text{rms}} \cdot \cos\phi $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Where $\cos\phi$ is the power factor, $\phi$ is the phase angle:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \tan\phi = \frac{X_L}{R} = \frac{\sqrt{3}R}{R} = \sqrt{3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \phi = 60^\circ $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \cos\phi = \cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>4. Substitute and Simplify</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P = E_{\text{rms}} \cdot I_{\text{rms}} \cdot \frac{1}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P = \left(\frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \left(\frac{E_0}{2R\sqrt{2}}\right) \frac{1}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Multiply the numerators and denominators:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = \frac{E_0 \cdot E_0}{\sqrt{2} \cdot 2R \cdot \sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = \frac{E_0^2}{2 \cdot 2R} \cdot \frac{1}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = \frac{E_0^2}{4R} \cdot \frac{1}{2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = \frac{E_0^2}{8R} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>The power consumed in the circuit is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\frac{E_0^2}{8R}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, the correct option is <prep-strong>Option C</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>An a.c. source is applied to a series LR circuit with $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}=3 \mathrm{R}$ and power factor is $\mathrm{X}_1$. Now a capacitor with $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm{R}$ is added in series to LR circuit and the power factor is $\mathrm{X}_2$. The ratio $\mathrm{X}_1$ to $\mathrm{X}_2$ is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>In the LR circuit, $X_L = 3R$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Power factor (without capacitor) is $X_1$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>When a capacitor is added, $X_C = R$, new power factor is $X_2$.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Asked: Find ratio $\dfrac{X_1}{X_2}$.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Power factor for LR circuit ($X_1$)</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Power factor, $X_1 = \cos \phi_1 = \dfrac{R}{Z_1}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Where,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ Z_1 = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L)^2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Given $X_L = 3R$, so</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ Z_1 = \sqrt{R^2 + (3R)^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + 9R^2} = \sqrt{10}R $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Therefore,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ X_1 = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{10}R} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Power factor for LCR circuit ($X_2$)</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, circuit is LCR in series.</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>$X_L = 3R$, $X_C = R$</prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Net reactance:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ X = X_L - X_C = 3R - R = 2R $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Impedance:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ Z_2 = \sqrt{R^2 + (X)^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + (2R)^2} = \sqrt{1R^2 + 4R^2} = \sqrt{5}R $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Power factor,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ X_2 = \cos \phi_2 = \dfrac{R}{Z_2} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{5}R} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Find the ratio $\dfrac{X_1}{X_2}$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{X_1}{X_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}}{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{10}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplify:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{10}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5 \times 2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \dfrac{X_1}{X_2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Or,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ X_1 : X_2 = 1 : \sqrt{2} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C: $1 : \sqrt{2}$</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A parallel beam of light is incident normally on a plane surface absorbing $50 \%$ of the light and reflecting the rest. If the incident beam carries 90 W of power, the force exerted by it on the surface is ( $\mathrm{C}=$ velocity of light in air $=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ )</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Power of incident light, $P = 90$ W  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Surface absorbs $50\%$ of the light and reflects $50\%$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Speed of light, $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Let's follow the <prep-strong>NCERT method</prep-strong>:</prep-p>
<prep-h3>Step 1: <prep-strong>Find the force due to absorption</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>When light is <prep-strong>absorbed</prep-strong>, the force exerted on the surface is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ F_{\text{abs}} = \frac{P_{\text{absorbed}}}{c} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since $50\%$ is absorbed:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P_{\text{absorbed}} = 0.5 \times 90 = 45~\text{W} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ F_{\text{abs}} = \frac{45}{3 \times 10^8} = 1.5 \times 10^{-7}~\text{N} $$</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: <prep-strong>Find the force due to reflection</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>When light is <prep-strong>reflected normally</prep-strong> (for normal incidence and perfect reflection), the change in momentum is <prep-strong>twice</prep-strong> that of absorption.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Force due to <prep-strong>reflection</prep-strong>:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ F_{\text{ref}} = \frac{2P_{\text{reflected}}}{c} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since $50\%$ is reflected:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P_{\text{reflected}} = 0.5 \times 90 = 45~\text{W} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ F_{\text{ref}} = \frac{2 \times 45}{3 \times 10^8} = \frac{90}{3 \times 10^8} = 3 \times 10^{-7}~\text{N} $$</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: <prep-strong>Total force exerted</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>$$ F_{\text{total}} = F_{\text{abs}} + F_{\text{ref}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ F_{\text{total}} = 1.5 \times 10^{-7}~\text{N} + 3 \times 10^{-7}~\text{N} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ F_{\text{total}} = 4.5 \times 10^{-7}~\text{N} $$</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$\boxed{4.5 \times 10^{-7}~\text{N}}$ (Option A)</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The maximum velocity of the photoelectrons emitted by a metal surface is $9 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The value of ratio of charge (e) to mass (m) of the photoelectron is $1.8 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{kg}$. The value of stopping potential in volt is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Maximum velocity of photoelectrons, $v_{max} = 9 \times 10^5~\text{m/s}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\dfrac{e}{m} = 1.8 \times 10^{11}~\text{C/kg}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Let the stopping potential be $V_0$.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Kinetic Energy of Photoelectron</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectron is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ K_{max} = \frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Stopping Potential Relation</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The stopping potential $V_0$ is related by the equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ eV_0 = K_{max} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V_0 = \frac{K_{max}}{e} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Substitute for $K_{max}/e$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute $K_{max}$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V_0 = \frac{\frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^2}{e} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>But $\frac{e}{m}$ is given.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{m}{e} = \frac{1}{\frac{e}{m}} = \frac{1}{1.8\times 10^{11}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V_0 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{m}{e} (v_{max})^2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Substitute Values</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$v_{max} = 9 \times 10^5~\text{m/s}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$m/e = \dfrac{1}{1.8 \times 10^{11}}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_0 = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{1.8 \times 10^{11}} \right) \left(9 \times 10^5\right)^2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 5: Calculate $(9 \times 10^5)^2$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ (9 \times 10^5)^2 = 81 \times 10^{10} = 8.1 \times 10^{11} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 6: Substitute and Calculate</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_0 = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{1.8 \times 10^{11}} \times (8.1 \times 10^{11}) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_0 = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{8.1 \times 10^{11}}{1.8 \times 10^{11}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_0 = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{8.1}{1.8} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_0 = \frac{1}{2} \times 4.5 = 2.25~\text{V} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: $2.25$</prep-strong> volts</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The ratio of energies of photons produced due to transition of electron of hydrogen atom from its (i) third to $2^{\text {nd }}$ energy level and (ii) highest energy level to $3^{\text {rd }}$ level is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-strong>Case (i):</prep-strong> Electron transition from $n=3 \to n=2$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Photon energy:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{n_2^2} - \frac{1}{n_1^2}\right)\ \text{eV}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E_{(3 \to 2)} = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{2^2} - \frac{1}{3^2}\right). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 13.6 \left(\frac{9 - 4}{36}\right). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 13.6 \cdot \frac{5}{36}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{68}{36} = \frac{17}{9}\ \text{eV}. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Case (ii):</prep-strong> Transition from highest energy level ($n = \infty$) to $n=3$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Energy of photon:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{3^2} - \frac{1}{\infty^2}\right). $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 13.6 \cdot \frac{1}{9}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{13.6}{9} = \frac{136}{90} = \frac{68}{45}\ \text{eV}. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Now ratio:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{E_{(3 \to 2)}}{E_{(\infty \to 3)}} = \frac{\tfrac{17}{9}}{\tfrac{68}{45}}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Simplify:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{17}{9} \cdot \frac{45}{68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{17 \cdot 45}{9 \cdot 68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{17 \cdot 5}{68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{85}{68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{85}{68}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Divide numerator and denominator by 17:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{5}{4}. $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{5:4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>That matches <prep-strong>Option B</prep-strong>. ✅</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>In hydrogen atom, transition from the state $\mathrm{n}=6$ to $n=1$ results in ultraviolet radiation. Infrared radiation will be obtained in the transition</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Recall hydrogen energy level formula</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>For hydrogen:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E_n = - \frac{13.6 \, \text{eV}}{n^2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>The energy of the photon emitted in a transition $n_i \to n_f$ is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{n_f^2} - \frac{1}{n_i^2}\right) \, \text{eV} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Ultraviolet vs Visible vs Infrared</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Large energy difference → higher frequency → shorter wavelength → ultraviolet.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Moderate energy difference → visible.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Small energy difference → longer wavelength → infrared.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Analyze options</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-strong>(A) $n=3 \to n=1$</prep-strong>:  </prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$\Delta E = 13.6 \left(1 - \frac{1}{9}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{8}{9} \approx 12.1 \, \text{eV}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>This corresponds to wavelength $\lambda \approx 1240/12.1 \approx 102 \,\text{nm}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>That is deep <prep-strong>UV</prep-strong>. Not IR.</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-strong>(B) $n=4 \to n=2$</prep-strong>:  </prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$\Delta E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{16}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{3}{16} = 2.55 \,\text{eV}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\lambda \approx 1240/2.55 \approx 486 \,\text{nm}$ → <prep-strong>visible (blue-green)</prep-strong>. Not IR.</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-strong>(C) $n=6 \to n=2$</prep-strong>:  </prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$\Delta E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{36}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{8}{36} \approx 3.02 \,\text{eV}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\lambda \approx 1240/3.02 \approx 410 \,\text{nm}$. <prep-strong>Visible (violet)</prep-strong>. Not IR.</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-strong>(D) $n=5 \to n=3$:</prep-strong>  </prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$\Delta E = 13.6 \left(\frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{25}\right) = 13.6 \times \frac{16}{225} = 0.967 \,\text{eV}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\lambda \approx 1240/0.967 \approx 1280 \,\text{nm}$. That's <prep-strong>Infrared</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

<prep-p>✅ <prep-strong>Correct Answer: Option D ($n=5 \to n=3$)</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the energy per mole of photon of electromagnetic radiation having wavelength $700 \mathrm{~nm}\left[\mathrm{~h}=6.626 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}, \mathrm{c}=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right]$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given data:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Wavelength, $\lambda = 700 \ \mathrm{nm} = 700 \times 10^{-9} \ \mathrm{m}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Planck’s constant, $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \ \mathrm{Js}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Speed of light, $c = 3 \times 10^8 \ \mathrm{m/s}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Avogadro’s number, $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23} \ \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Energy of one photon</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The energy of one photon is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E = \frac{6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8}{700 \times 10^{-9}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate numerator and denominator separately:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Numerator: $6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^8 = 1.9878 \times 10^{-25}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Denominator: $700 \times 10^{-9} = 7 \times 10^{2} \times 10^{-9} = 7 \times 10^{-7}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E = \frac{1.9878 \times 10^{-25}}{7 \times 10^{-7}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E = \frac{1.9878}{7} \times 10^{-25+7} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E \approx 0.284 \times 10^{-18} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ E = 2.84 \times 10^{-19} \ \mathrm{J} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Energy per mole of photon</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Multiply by Avogadro's number to get energy per mole:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Energy per mole} = E \times N_A $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 2.84 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2.84 \times 6.022 = 17.106 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 10^{-19} \times 10^{23} = 10^{4} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Energy per mole} = 17.106 \times 10^{4} \ \mathrm{J} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = 1.71 \times 10^{5} \ \mathrm{J} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{1.71 \times 10^{5} \ \text{J}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option:</prep-strong> Option A</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Wave particle duality of electromagnetic radiation

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Identify the compound formed from elements X, Y, Z having oxidation state +2, +5, $$-$$2 respectively.</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To determine the correct compound formed from elements X, Y, and Z with oxidation states +2, +5, and -2 respectively, we need to balance the charges in the compound such that the total charge is zero.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Let's denote the oxidation states of X, Y, and Z as follows:</prep-p>

<prep-p>X: +2</prep-p>

<prep-p>Y: +5</prep-p>

<prep-p>Z: -2</prep-p>

<prep-p>Now we will analyze each option to see if the total charge equals zero.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A: $$\mathrm{X\left(Y_4 Z\right)}$$</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>In this case, the compound is $$\mathrm{X Y_4 Z}$$.</prep-p>

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of X: +2</prep-li>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of Y: $$+5 \times 4 = +20$$</prep-li>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of Z: -2</prep-li>

<prep-li>Total charge: $$+2 + 20 - 2 = +20$$</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

<prep-p>This compound does not balance to zero, so it is not correct.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: $$\mathrm{X_3 \left(Y Z_4 \right)_2}$$</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>In this case, the compound is $$\mathrm{X_3 \left(Y Z_4\right)_2}$$.</prep-p>

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of 3X: $$+2 \times 3 = +6$$</prep-li>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of 2Y: $$+5 \times 2 = +10$$</prep-li>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of $$8Z: -2 \times 8 = -16$$</prep-li>

<prep-li>Total charge: $$+6 + 10 - 16 = 0$$</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

<prep-p>This compound balances to zero, so it is a possible correct answer.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C: $$\mathrm{X_3 \left(Y Z_2 \right)_2}$$</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>In this case, the compound is $$\mathrm{X_3 \left(Y Z_2 \right)_2}$$.</prep-p>

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of 3X: $$+2 \times 3 = +6$$</prep-li>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of 2Y: $$+5 \times 2 = +10$$</prep-li>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of 4Z: $$-2 \times 4 = -8$$</prep-li>

<prep-li>Total charge: $$+6 + 10 - 8 = +8$$</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

<prep-p>This compound does not balance to zero, so it is not correct.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option D: XYZ$$_2$$</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>In this case, the compound is XYZ$$_2$$.</prep-p>

<prep-ul>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of X: +2</prep-li>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of Y: +5</prep-li>

<prep-li>Oxidation state of 2Z: $$-2 \times 2 = -4$$</prep-li>

<prep-li>Total charge: $$+2 + 5 - 4 = +3$$</prep-li>

</prep-ul>

<prep-p>This compound does not balance to zero, so it is not correct.</prep-p>

<prep-p>Therefore, the correct option is:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: $$\mathrm{X_3 \left(Y Z_4 \right)_2}$$</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A compound contains atoms of $x, y$ and z elements. Oxidation numbers of $x, y$ and $z$ are +3 , +5 and -2 respectively. Identify the possible formula of this compound.</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let the oxidation numbers be:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$x = +3$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$y = +5$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$z = -2$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>For a compound to be neutral, the sum of the oxidation numbers (overall charge) must be $0$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Let us check all options one by one.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Option A: $\mathrm{XYZ}_2$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Total oxidation number:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ (+3) + (+5) + 2 \times (-2) = 3 + 5 - 4 = 4 \neq 0 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Not neutral. <prep-strong>Not possible</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-h3>Option B: $\mathrm{Y}_2\left(\mathrm{XZ}_3\right)_2$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>First, expand the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$Y$: $2$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$X$: $2$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$Z$: $3 \times 2 = 6$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Total oxidation number:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2 \times (+5) + 2 \times (+3) + 6 \times (-2) = 10 + 6 - 12 = 4 \neq 0 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Not neutral. <prep-strong>Not possible</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-h3>Option C: $\mathrm{X}_3\left(\mathrm{YZ}_4\right)_3$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Expand the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$X$: $3$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$Y$: $3$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$Z$: $4 \times 3 = 12$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Total oxidation number:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 3 \times (+3) + 3 \times (+5) + 12 \times (-2) = 9 + 15 - 24 = 0 $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Sum is zero (neutral). This is possible.</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-h3>Option D: $\mathrm{X}_3\left(\mathrm{Y}_4\mathrm{Z}\right)_2$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Expand the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$X$: $3$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$Y$: $4 \times 2 = 8$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$Z$: $2$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Total oxidation number:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 3 \times (+3) + 8 \times (+5) + 2 \times (-2) = 9 + 40 - 4 = 45 \neq 0 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Not neutral. <prep-strong>Not possible</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-h3><prep-strong>Final Answer</prep-strong></prep-h3>
<prep-p>The possible formula of the compound is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\mathrm{X}_3\left(\mathrm{YZ}_4\right)_3} $</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the volume of a gas at $1.032 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~Nm}^{-2}$ if it occupies $1 \mathrm{~dm}^3$ of volume at normal temperature and pressure?</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The relationship between pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature is described by Boyle's Law, which states that the product of the initial pressure and volume is equal to the product of the final pressure and volume. Mathematically, this can be expressed as:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$ P_1 $ is the initial pressure (normal atmospheric pressure, approximately $1.013 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^{-2}$),</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ V_1 $ is the initial volume ($1 \, \text{dm}^3$),</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ P_2 $ is the final pressure ($1.032 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^{-2}$),</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ V_2 $ is the final volume.</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Rearranging the formula to solve for $ V_2 $:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V_2 = \frac{P_1 V_1}{P_2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting the known values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_2 = \frac{(1.013 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^{-2}) \times (1 \, \text{dm}^3)}{1.032 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^{-2}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_2 = \frac{1.013 \times 10^5}{1.032 \times 10^5} \, \text{dm}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_2 = \frac{1.013}{1.032} \, \text{dm}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_2 \approx 0.982 \, \text{dm}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the volume of the gas at $1.032 \times 10^5 \, \text{Nm}^{-2}$ is approximately $0.982 \, \text{dm}^3$. Hence, the correct option is:</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A: 0.982 dm$ ^3 $</prep-strong></prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Gases law: Boyle's law, Charles' law, Gay Lussac's law, Avogadro's law

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>How many moles of dioxygen are present in $8.314 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^3$ of it at 318 K having pressure $3.18 \times 10^5 \mathrm{Nm}^{-2} ?\left(\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To find the number of moles of dioxygen, use the ideal gas equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ PV = nRT $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>$ P = 3.18 \times 10^5 \, \text{N/m}^2 $ (Pressure)</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ V = 8.314 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{m}^3 $ (Volume)</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ n $ is the number of moles (what we are solving for)</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ R = 8.314 \, \text{J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1} $ (Ideal gas constant)</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>$ T = 318 \, \text{K} $ (Temperature)</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Rearrange the ideal gas equation to solve for $ n $:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ n = \frac{PV}{RT} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the known values into the equation:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ n = \frac{(3.18 \times 10^5) \times (8.314 \times 10^{-3})}{8.314 \times 318} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate the numerator:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 3.18 \times 10^5 \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3} = 2644.602 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Calculate the denominator:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 8.314 \times 318 = 2645.652 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, calculate $ n $:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ n = \frac{2644.602}{2645.652} \approx 0.9996 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the number of moles of dioxygen is approximately $ 1 $ mole. Therefore, the correct answer is:</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: 1.0 mole</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the volume occupied by all particles in fcc unit cell if volume of unit cell is $1.6 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~cm}^3$.</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Number of atoms in an fcc unit cell</prep-h3>
<prep-p>In an <prep-strong>fcc structure</prep-strong>, the effective number of atoms in a unit cell = 4.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Relation between atomic radius and edge length</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For fcc,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ a = \frac{4r}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2} \cdot 2r $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ r = \frac{a}{2\sqrt{2}} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Find edge length from unit cell volume</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ a^3 = V_{\text{cell}} = 1.6 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ a = (1.6 \times 10^{-23})^{1/3} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Cube root of $1.6 \approx 1.17$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Cube root of $10^{-23} = 10^{-7.667} \approx 2.15 \times 10^{-8}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ a \approx 1.17 \times 2.15 \times 10^{-8} \approx 2.51 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{cm} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Calculate radius</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ r = \frac{a}{2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2.51 \times 10^{-8}}{2 \times 1.414} = \frac{2.51 \times 10^{-8}}{2.828} \approx 8.88 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{cm} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 5: Volume of one atom (as a sphere)</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ V_{\text{atom}} = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ r^3 = (8.88 \times 10^{-9})^3 \approx 7.0 \times 10^{-25} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_{\text{atom}} \approx \frac{4}{3}\pi \times 7.0 \times 10^{-25} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_{\text{atom}} \approx 2.93 \times 10^{-24}\ \text{cm}^3 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 6: Total volume of atoms in unit cell</prep-h3>
<prep-p>4 atoms per cell:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_{\text{total}} = 4 \times V_{\text{atom}} = 4 \times 2.93 \times 10^{-24} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ V_{\text{total}} \approx 1.17 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 7: Match with options</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Closest value is  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C: $1.184 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3$</prep-strong> ✅</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{1.184 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3} $ (Option C)</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Number of particles in cubic unit cells

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The mass of an atom present in unit cell is $4.4 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~g}$ and the product of density and volume of unit cell is $1.792 \times 10^{-22} \mathrm{~g}$. What is the type of cubic unit cell?</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Mass of atom in the unit cell, $m = 4.4 \times 10^{-23}$ g  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Density $\times$ Volume of unit cell $= 1.792 \times 10^{-22}$ g</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Let number of atoms per unit cell $= z$.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Relation between mass, $z$, and unit cell</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>The total mass in a unit cell:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Total mass in unit cell} = z \times m $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Density formula for a unit cell</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>For a cubic unit cell,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Density} = \frac{z \times m}{a^3} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Density} \times a^3 = z \times m $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>But it is given that,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text{Density} \times a^3 = 1.792 \times 10^{-22} \text{ g} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ z \times m = 1.792 \times 10^{-22} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Calculate $z$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Given $m = 4.4 \times 10^{-23}$ g:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ z = \frac{1.792 \times 10^{-22}}{4.4 \times 10^{-23}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Divide numerator and denominator:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ z = \frac{1.792}{4.4} \times \frac{10^{-22}}{10^{-23}} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = 0.407 \times 10^{1} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ = 4.07 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since $z$ must be a whole number and is closest to $4$,</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Type of cubic unit cell</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Simple cubic: $z = 1$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Body centred (BCC): $z = 2$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Face centred (FCC): $z = 4$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Base centred: $z = 2$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So, $z = 4$ indicates a <prep-strong>face centred cubic (FCC) unit cell</prep-strong>.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\text{Face centred unit cell}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B is correct.</prep-strong></prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Number of particles in cubic unit cells

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Arrange the following solutions according to decreasing order of osmotic pressure under similar condition of temperature and assuming complete dissociation.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{array}{|c|l|} \hline \text { I. } & 0.2 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{KCl} \\ \hline \text { II. } & 0.3 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{MgSO}_4 \\ \hline \text { III. } & 0.1 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{BaCl}_2 \\ \hline \text { IV. } & 0.5 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{Al}_2\left(\mathrm{SO}_4\right)_3 \\ \hline \end{array} $$</prep-p>

    <prep-td class="tg-baqh">$$<prep-br>\begin{aligned}<prep-br>& 0.1 \mathrm{~m} \\<prep-br>& \mathrm{BaCl}_2<prep-br>\end{aligned}<prep-br>$$</prep-td>
    <prep-td class="tg-baqh">$$<prep-br>\mathrm{BaCl}_2 \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Ba}^{2+}]{ }+2 \mathrm{Cl}^{-}<prep-br>$$</prep-td>
    <prep-td class="tg-baqh">$$<prep-br>3 \times 0.1=0.3 \mathrm{~m}<prep-br>$$</prep-td>

<prep-p>Hence, $\mathrm{Al}_2\left(\mathrm{SO}_4\right)_3$ solution gives more number of particles and has the highest osmotic pressure among the given. So, the correct order of increasing osmotic pressure is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{IV}>\mathrm{II}>\mathrm{I}>\mathrm{III} . $$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: Find molar mass of nonvolatile solute when 20 g of it dissolved in 200 g water at 300 K . [Relative lowering of vapour pressure $=0.02$ ]
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Mass of solute, $w_2 = 20\,\text{g}$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Mass of solvent (water), $w_1 = 200\,\text{g}$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Relative lowering of vapour pressure, $\dfrac{\Delta p}{p^0} = 0.02$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Molar mass of solvent (water), $M_1 = 18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Let molar mass of solute be $M_2$ (to be found).</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Write formula for relative lowering of vapour pressure</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>According to Raoult's law (NCERT formula),</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Relative lowering of vapour pressure} = \frac{\Delta p}{p^0} = \frac{n_2}{n_1 + n_2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>For dilute solutions, $n_2 \ll n_1$, so</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{\Delta p}{p^0} \approx \frac{n_2}{n_1} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Where $n_2$ = moles of solute, $n_1$ = moles of solvent.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Write moles in terms of mass and molar mass</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n_2 = \frac{w_2}{M_2} \qquad n_1 = \frac{w_1}{M_1} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Rightarrow \frac{\Delta p}{p^0} = \frac{\dfrac{w_2}{M_2}}{\dfrac{w_1}{M_1}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{w_2}{M_2} \cdot \frac{M_1}{w_1} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ = \frac{w_2 M_1}{w_1 M_2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Substitute values and solve for $M_2$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 0.02 = \frac{20 \times 18}{200 \times M_2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 0.02 = \frac{360}{200 \times M_2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 0.02 \times 200 \times M_2 = 360 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 4 M_2 = 360 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ M_2 = \frac{360}{4} = 90~\text{g mol}^{-1} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Option C  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\boxed{90~\mathrm{g}~\mathrm{mol}^{-1}}$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Calculate the ionisation constant of $0.08 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{dm}{ }^{-3}$ of a monobasic acid having $\mathrm{pH}=2$.</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-strong>Given:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Concentration of acid, $C = 0.08 \,\text{mol dm}^{-3}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>pH = 2 (so solution is acidic)</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 1: Calculate $[H^+]$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \text{pH} = -\log [H^+] $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ [H^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-2} = 0.01 \,\text{M} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Degree of dissociation ($\alpha$)</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The acid dissociates: $HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$</prep-p>
<prep-p>If total acid concentration is $C = 0.08\,\text{M}$, then:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ [H^+] = C \alpha \implies \alpha = \frac{[H^+]}{C} = \frac{0.01}{0.08} = 0.125 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Expression for $K_a$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ K_a = \frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since it is monobasic:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ [H^+] = [A^-] = 0.01\,\text{M}, \quad [HA] = C - \alpha C = 0.08 - 0.01 = 0.07 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K_a = \frac{(0.01)(0.01)}{0.07} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Simplify</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ K_a = \frac{1 \times 10^{-4}}{0.07} \approx 1.43 \times 10^{-3} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 5: Match with options</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Closest is:</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option D: $1.25 \times 10^{-3}$</prep-strong> ✅</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{1.25 \times 10^{-3}} $</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Dissociation constant of weak acids and weak bases

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Calculate the equilibrium concentration of $\mathrm{Pb}^{++}$ions in a solution of PbS containing $1 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{dm}^{-3}$ of sulphide ions.</prep-p>
<prep-p>(Given $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}$ for $\mathrm{PbS}=8.0 \times 10^{-28}$ )</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Write the dissociation equation for PbS</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{PbS}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Pb}^{2+}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + \mathrm{S}^{2-}_{(\mathrm{aq})} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: Write the solubility product ($K_{sp}$) expression</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}} = [\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}] [\mathrm{S}^{2-}] $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 3: Substitute the given values</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>We are told that $[\mathrm{S}^{2-}] = 1 \times 10^{-11}$ mol dm$^{-3}$ and $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}} = 8.0 \times 10^{-28}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Put these values into the $K_{sp}$ formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 8.0 \times 10^{-28} = [\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}] \times 1 \times 10^{-11} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 4: Solve for $[\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}]$</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Divide both sides by $1 \times 10^{-11}$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ [\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}] = \frac{8.0 \times 10^{-28}}{1 \times 10^{-11}} = 8 \times 10^{-17} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Final Answer:</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The equilibrium concentration of $\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}$ ions in the solution is $8 \times 10^{-17}$ mol dm$^{-3}$.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Calculate the standard enthalpy change of following reaction.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{CH}_{4(\mathrm{~s})}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)} \\ & \text { if } \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{-}\left(\mathrm{CH}_4\right)=-75 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^*\left(\mathrm{CO}_2\right)=-390 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)=-286 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Write the Reaction and Formula</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The reaction is: 

$$ \mathrm{CH}_{4(\mathrm{~s})}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(\ell)} $$

We use this formula to find the enthalpy change:

$$ \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} = \sum \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} (\text{Products}) - \sum \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} (\text{Reactants}) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: List the Given Enthalpies of Formation</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$ \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} (\mathrm{CH}_4) = -75~\mathrm{kJ~mol}^{-1} $$

$$ \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{*} (\mathrm{CO}_2) = -390~\mathrm{kJ~mol}^{-1} $$

$$ \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} (\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}) = -286~\mathrm{kJ~mol}^{-1} $$

For elements like $ \mathrm{O}_2 $, $ \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} $ is always 0.

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 3: Plug in the Values</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

First, add up the enthalpies for the products:

$$ (-390) + 2 \times (-286) $$

Then, add up the enthalpies for the reactants:

$$ (-75) + 0 \text{ (for } \mathrm{O}_2) $$

So,

$$ \Delta_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ} = [(-390) + 2(-286)] - [(-75) + 0] $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 4: Do the Calculations</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

Calculate the numbers:

<prep-br>

$2 \times (-286) = -572$

<prep-br>

So the sum for products is:

$$ -390 - 572 = -962 $$

<prep-br>

For reactants: $-75$

<prep-br>

Now, subtract:

$$ -962 - (-75) = -962 + 75 = -887 $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 5: State the Final Answer</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>

The standard enthalpy change for the reaction is:

$$ -887~\mathrm{kJ} $$

</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Standard enthalpy of reaction from standard enthalpies of formation

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Calculate the standard enthalpy change for reaction,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{OH}_{(l)}+3 \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{~g})} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \\ & \text { if } \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{OH}\right)=-280 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{CO}_2\right)=-390 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ & \Delta_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{H}^{\circ}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)=-285 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Write the reaction and important values</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The reaction is: $$\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}_{(l)}+3\ \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \longrightarrow 2\ \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+3\ \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_{(l)}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>We are given these standard enthalpy values (in kJ mol<prep-sup>−1</prep-sup>):</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}) = -280$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\mathrm{CO}_2) = -390$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}) = -285$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The enthalpy of formation for $$\mathrm{O}_2$$ is 0, since it is an element in its standard state.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: Write the formula for enthalpy change</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>The standard enthalpy change of the reaction ($$\Delta H^\circ$$) is calculated like this:</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$ \Delta H^\circ = [\text{Sum of enthalpies of products}] - [\text{Sum of enthalpies of reactants}] $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

For this reaction:

$$ \Delta H^\circ = [2 \Delta_\mathrm{f} H^\circ(\mathrm{CO}_2) + 3 \Delta_\mathrm{f} H^\circ(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})] - [\Delta_\mathrm{f} H^\circ(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{OH}) + 3 \Delta_\mathrm{f} H^\circ(\mathrm{O}_2)] $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 3: Substitute values and calculate</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Now put in the numbers:</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$ = [2 \times (-390) + 3 \times (-285)] - [(-280) + 3 \times 0] $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

Calculate inside the brackets:

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$ = [(-780) + (-855)] - (-280) $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

Now add and subtract:

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$ = -1635 - (-280) $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

Subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive:

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$ = -1635 + 280 = -1355~\mathrm{kJ} $$

</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Standard enthalpy of reaction from standard enthalpies of formation

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>If standard reduction potential $\left(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}\right)$ of $\left(\mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})}\right),\left(\mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+} \mid \mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{s})}\right),\left(\mathrm{Zn}^{+2}{ }_{(\mathrm{aq})} \mid \mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})}\right)$ and $\left(\mathrm{Cu}^{+2}{ }_{(\text {aq })} \mid \mathrm{Cu}_{(\text {s })}\right)$ are $-2.37 \mathrm{~V},+0.79 \mathrm{~V},-0.76 \mathrm{~V}$ and +0.34 V respectively. Which of the following reaction is spontaneous?</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>For reaction to be spontaneous, $\mathrm{E}_{\text {Cell }}^0$ should be positive.</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{E}_{\text {Cell }}^0=\mathrm{E}_{\text {cathode }}^0-\mathrm{E}_{\text {anode }}^0 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text {  } \begin{array}{ll}(A)  & \mathrm{E}_{\text {Cell }}^0=\mathrm{E}_{\left(\mathrm{Mg}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{Mg}\right)}^0-\mathrm{E}_{\left(\mathrm{Zn}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{Zn}\right)}^0 \\ & =-2.37 \mathrm{~V}-(-0.76) \mathrm{V}=-1.61 \mathrm{~V} \end{array} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text { } \begin{aligned} (B) &\,\,\, \mathrm{E}_{\text {Cell }}^0=\mathrm{E}_{\left(\mathrm{Zn}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{Zn}\right)}^0-\mathrm{E}_{\left(\mathrm{Ag}^{+} \mid \mathrm{Ag}^{-}\right)}^0 \\ & =-0.76 \mathrm{~V}-(+0.79) \mathrm{V}=-1.55 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text {  } \begin{aligned}(C) &\,\,\, \mathrm{E}_{\text {Cell }}^0=\mathrm{E}_{\left(\mathrm{Cu}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{ICu}\right)}^0-\mathrm{E}_{\left(\mathrm{Zn}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{Zn}\right)}^0 \\ & =0.34 \mathrm{~V}-(-0.76) \mathrm{V}=+1.1 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \text {  }  \begin{aligned}(D) &\,\,\, \mathrm{E}_{\text {Cell }}^0=\mathrm{E}_{\left(\mathrm{Mg}^{+2}{ }_{1 \mathrm{Mg}}\right)}^0-\mathrm{E}_{\left(\mathrm{Cu}^{+2} \mid \mathrm{Cu}\right)}^0 \\ & =-2.37 \mathrm{~V}+0.34 \mathrm{~V}=-2.03 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Only the reaction in Option C has a positive standard cell potential, indicating it is spontaneous.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>If standard emf of cell $\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{s})}\left|\mathrm{Zn}_{(\mathrm{iM})}^{+2}\right| \mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{iM})}^{+1} \mid \mathrm{Ag}_{(\mathrm{s})}$ is 1.55 V .</prep-p>
<prep-p>What is electrical work done under standard conditions?</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Standard emf of cell, $E^\circ_{cell} = 1.55\,\text{V}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Cell: $\mathrm{Zn_{(s)}|Zn^{2+}_{(1\,M)}||Ag^{+}_{(1\,M)}|Ag_{(s)}}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Write the cell reaction and find $n$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \begin{align*} \text{At anode (oxidation):} &\ \mathrm{Zn(s)} \to \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2e^- \\ \text{At cathode (reduction):} &\ \mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + e^- \to \mathrm{Ag(s)} \\ \end{align*} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>To balance electrons, multiply the cathode reaction by 2:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ 2\,\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + 2e^- \to 2\,\mathrm{Ag(s)} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Overall cell reaction:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mathrm{Zn(s)} + 2\,\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \to \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + 2\,\mathrm{Ag(s)} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, number of electrons transferred, $n = 2$.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Formula for maximum electrical work</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Electrical work done under standard conditions is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -nF E^\circ_{\text{cell}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Where,</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$n$ = number of moles of electrons exchanged $(=2)$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$F$ = Faraday’s constant $(=96,500~\text{C/mol})$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ = emf of the cell $(=1.55~\text{V})$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Substitute and calculate</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 96,500 \times 1.55 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 149,575 = -299,150~\text{J} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Convert J to kJ:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \Delta G^\circ = \frac{-299,150}{1000}~\text{kJ} = -299.15~\text{kJ} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>The correct answer is:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{-299.150~\text{kJ}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option C</prep-strong> is correct.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>The rate constant for a first order reaction is $0.58 \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at 300 K and $0.026 \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ at 290 K .</prep-p>
<prep-p>What is the energy of activation?</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \left(\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right) $$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{k}_2}{\mathrm{k}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 \mathrm{R}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1}{\mathrm{~T}_1 \mathrm{~T}_2}\right)\\ &\text { Substituting the given values }\\ &\begin{aligned} \log _{10} \frac{0.58}{0.026}=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 \times 8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}} &  \times\left[\frac{300 \mathrm{~K}-290 \mathrm{~K}}{290 \mathrm{~K} \times 300 \mathrm{~K}}\right] \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \log _{10} 22.307=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 \times 8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}} \times \frac{10}{290 \times 300} \\ & 1.3484=\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{19.15 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}} \times 1.15 \times 10^{-4} \\ & \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}} & =\frac{1.3484 \times 19.15}{1.15 \times 10^{-4}} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ & \quad=224538 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\ & \approx 224.55 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>Half life of a first order reaction is 900 minute at 400 K , find its half life at 300 K ?</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \left(\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{a}}}{2.303 \mathrm{R}}=1.3056 \times 10^3\right) $$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Given data:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Half-life at $400\,\text{K}$, $t_{1/2,1} = 900\, \text{min}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$E_a / (2.303R) = 1.3056 \times 10^3$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Temperature 1: $T_1 = 400\,\text{K}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Temperature 2: $T_2 = 300\,\text{K}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>We are to find $t_{1/2,2}$ at $300\,\text{K}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Recall the half-life formula for a first-order reaction:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{k} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Use the Arrhenius equation in its logarithmic form:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \log \left( \frac{k_2}{k_1} \right) = \frac{E_a}{2.303R} \left( \frac{T_1 - T_2}{T_1 T_2} \right) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Relate half-lives to rate constants:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{t_{1/2,2}}{t_{1/2,1}} = \frac{k_1}{k_2} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 4: Substitute values into the Arrhenius expression:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Given,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \log \left( \frac{k_2}{k_1} \right) = \frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left( \frac{400-300}{400 \times 300} \right) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \log \left( \frac{k_2}{k_1} \right) = 1.3056 \times 10^3 \times \left( \frac{100}{120000} \right) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \log \left( \frac{k_2}{k_1} \right) = 1.3056 \times 10^3 \times \frac{1}{1200} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \log \left( \frac{k_2}{k_1} \right) = \frac{1.3056 \times 10^3}{1200} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \log \left( \frac{k_2}{k_1} \right) = 1.088 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 5: Write $k_1/k_2$:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \log \left( \frac{k_1}{k_2} \right) = -1.088 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{k_1}{k_2} = 10^{-1.088} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 6: Relate half-lives:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \frac{t_{1/2,2}}{t_{1/2,1}} = \frac{k_1}{k_2} = 10^{-1.088} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ t_{1/2,2} = t_{1/2,1} \times 10^{1.088} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 7: Calculate $10^{1.088}$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>First, </prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ 10^{1.088} \approx 12.25 $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 8: Calculate $t_{1/2,2}$</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ t_{1/2,2} = 900 \times 12.25 = 11025\, \text{min} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>Option <prep-strong>B</prep-strong> $11025.0$ minute</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Half life of the first order reactions (t1/2)

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Which lanthanoid from following may exhibit +4 oxidation state with $f^0$ configuration?</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall electronic configurations of neutral atoms</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Ce (Z = 58):</prep-strong> [Xe]$4f^1 5d^1 6s^2$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Eu (Z = 63):</prep-strong> [Xe]$4f^7 6s^2$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Tb (Z = 65):</prep-strong> [Xe]$4f^9 6s^2$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Lu (Z = 71):</prep-strong> [Xe]$4f^{14} 5d^1 6s^2$  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Consider +4 oxidation state</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Remove 4 electrons, preferentially from $6s$, then $5d$, then $4f$.</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Ce$^{4+}$:</prep-strong> Neutral = [Xe]$4f^1 5d^1 6s^2$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove 2 from 6s → [Xe]$4f^1 5d^1$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove 1 from 5d → [Xe]$4f^1$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove last from 4f → [Xe].  </prep-p>
<prep-p>→ <prep-strong><prep-em>So Ce$^{4+}$ has $f^0$.</prep-em></prep-strong></prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Eu$^{4+}$:</prep-strong> Neutral = [Xe]$4f^7 6s^2$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove 2 from 6s → [Xe]$4f^7$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove 2 from 4f → [Xe]$4f^5$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>→ Not $f^0$.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Tb$^{4+}$:</prep-strong> Neutral = [Xe]$4f^9 6s^2$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove 2 from 6s → [Xe]$4f^9$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove 2 more from 4f → [Xe]$4f^7$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>→ Not $f^0$.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Lu$^{4+}$:</prep-strong> Neutral = [Xe]$4f^{14} 5d^1 6s^2$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove 2 from 6s → [Xe]$4f^{14} 5d^1$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove 1 from 5d → [Xe]$4f^{14}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Remove 1 from 4f → [Xe]$4f^{13}$.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>→ Not $f^0$.  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Conclusion</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Only <prep-strong>Ce$^{4+}$</prep-strong> achieves the $f^0$ configuration.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>✅ <prep-strong>Answer: Option C (Ce)</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: Which from following cations develops lowest value of spin only magnetic moment?
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>To solve this, we use the <prep-strong>spin-only magnetic moment formula</prep-strong>:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} \, \text{BM} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $n$ = number of unpaired electrons.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 1: Find electronic configuration for each cation</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>(A) $\mathrm{V^{3+}}$</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Atomic number of V = 23 → configuration = [Ar] $3d^3 4s^2$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Removing 3 electrons (2 from 4s, 1 from 3d) → [Ar] $3d^2$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>→ Unpaired electrons = 2</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>(B) $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Atomic number of Cr = 24 → configuration = [Ar] $3d^5 4s^1$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Removing 3 electrons (first 4s and then 2 from 3d) → [Ar] $3d^3$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>→ Unpaired electrons = 3</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>(C) $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Atomic number of Mn = 25 → configuration = [Ar] $3d^5 4s^2$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Removing 2 electrons (from 4s) → [Ar] $3d^5$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>→ Unpaired electrons = 5</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>(D) $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Atomic number of Fe = 26 → configuration = [Ar] $3d^6 4s^2$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Removing 2 electrons (from 4s) → [Ar] $3d^6$  </prep-p>
<prep-p>→ Unpaired electrons = 4</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Calculate spin-only magnetic moment</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>For $\mathrm{V^{3+}}$ ($n=2$):  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83 \, \text{BM}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>For $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ ($n=3$):  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\mu = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87 \, \text{BM}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>For $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ ($n=5$):  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92 \, \text{BM}$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>For $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ ($n=4$):  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$\mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90 \, \text{BM}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 3: Compare values</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\mathrm{V^{3+}}$: ~2.83 BM (lowest)  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$: ~3.87 BM  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$: ~4.90 BM  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$: ~5.92 BM  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\mathrm{V^{3+}}} $ develops the lowest value of spin-only magnetic moment.</prep-p>
